post.running_head: the imam who spent nineteen years in custody
post.caption:
Al-Sindi b. Shahik ran the prison where Musa b. Ja'far died. He did not
bury the body. He walked the jurists of Baghdad past it, had them state
that they saw no wound, then carried it to the bridge and invited the
city to look at the face.

A man does not stage a viewing to prove a death nobody doubts.

Sources are named on the slides. Every figure traces to a page in the
edition cited, and where the chronicles differ the slides say so.

slides.body: the bridge at baghdad
Why did the men who held Musa b. Ja'far need a crowd to look at his face?

Al-Mufid puts the death of Musa b. Ja'far in the prison of al-Sindi b. Shahik at Baghdad. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the date and the age at death, Irshad p. 407]]. The jailer did not bury him. He sent for the jurists of the city and for its notable men, walked them past the body, and asked them to say what they saw. They saw no wound. They saw no mark of strangling. Al-Sindi took their testimony, wrote it down, and only then had the body carried out of the prison.

Out of the prison, and onto the bridge. Al-Sindi's men set the body down in the open and called the city to come and look at the face of Musa b. Ja'far. [[NEEDS CLAIM: who al-Sindi named among the witnesses on the bridge, Irshad p. 427]]. A jailer with a corpse he cannot explain buries it at night. This jailer did the opposite of hiding, and he did it in the most public place in Baghdad.

The face was the whole point. Al-Sindi needed Baghdad to carry away one sentence: I saw him, and he was dead. He was answering a claim that had been running through the city while Musa b. Ja'far was still alive. [[NEEDS CLAIM: how long before the death the claim of a hidden imamate is first attested]]. Al-Mufid states the claim without softening it. A group held that this man would not die at all.

The claim was that Musa b. Ja'far was the awaited one, and that he would hold the office for the rest of time. Al-Mufid reports it in those words at the point where he explains the viewing. A man who cannot die cannot leave a successor, so the claim was not devotional decoration. It decided who received the money, who gave the orders, and who inherited the network that ran from Medina to Kufa.

That network is what put him in custody in the first place. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the year of the first arrest and the caliph who ordered it]]. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the total years Musa b. Ja'far spent in custody, and the arithmetic behind the figure of nineteen]]. He was moved between Medina, Basra and Baghdad. Each move handed him to a different jailer, and each jailer inherited the same problem: a prisoner whose followers counted his absence as proof rather than as a defeat.

Harun al-Rashid solved the problem by sending a minister. Al-Mufid has Yahya b. Khalid arrive at Baghdad giving out that he had come to inspect the tax administration of the Sawad. He spent a few days on the paperwork. Then he sent for al-Sindi b. Shahik and gave him his instructions concerning the prisoner. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the date of Yahya b. Khalid's journey to Baghdad, and by whose order]].

Here the two accounts differ. Al-Mufid gives the poison as something reported to him and marks it as such: it is said that it went into dates, that Musa b. Ja'far ate them, that a fever held him three days. The Arabic chronicle of al-Tabari enters the death at Baghdad in its year and says nothing of poison at all. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what al-Tabari's notice states in full, Arabic text at 8:271]]. Two men writing about one prisoner, and one of them declines to name a cause.

The disagreement is the reason the viewing happened. Al-Sindi did not need a testimony against the charge of poison, which is a charge the jurists on the bridge could not have answered by looking. He needed a testimony against the charge that there was no body. Those are different accusations and they call for different theatre. He staged the one that fitted the second.

Al-Mufid keeps one refusal in the record. Al-Sindi asked to shroud the body himself. Musa b. Ja'far refused him and named a retainer of his own household to wash and prepare it. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the name of the retainer, Irshad p. 428]]. A prisoner who arranges his own burial expects to be buried. That expectation sits against the claim his followers were making on his behalf outside the wall.

The succession went to 'Ali b. Musa al-Rida, the eldest and the most prominent of thirty-seven children. [[NEEDS CLAIM: al-Rida's age at his father's death]]. He took an inheritance that came with agents, deposits and standing instructions across three provinces. Some of the men holding that money had spent nineteen years relaying it into a prison. When the prison emptied, the accounts stayed open.

Those men did not all accept the son. A part of the following stopped at the father, held that he had not died, and waited. Later writers call them the Waqifa, the ones who halted. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the earliest source that uses the name Waqifa, and its date]]. Their names survive in the chains of al-Kafi, where a transmitter is marked as belonging to the sect before his report is given.

Al-Kulayni's chains preserve one of them changing his mind. A companion says that he came to Khurasan while he was a member of the Waqifa and then left it. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the full text and page of the Khurasan report, al-Kafi]]. The compiler kept the label on the man rather than erasing it. He wanted a reader to weigh the report knowing who carried it, which is what a chain is for.

Al-Rida inherited the argument along with the office. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what al-Rida is reported to have said about his father's death, 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida]]. The dispute ran on inside the community for [[NEEDS CLAIM: how long the Waqifa persisted as a distinct group]], and it ran on in the sources long after the men who started it died, which is why a compiler two generations later still had to label a transmitter.
Al-Sindi b. Shahik put a face on a bridge to end an argument about whether a man had died, and the argument outlived the jailer, the caliph and the prison.

post.running_head: the imam who spent nineteen years in custody
post.caption:
Al-Kulayni ends his notice on Musa b. Ja'far with an address: buried at
Baghdad, in the graveyard of Quraysh. A grave is a fact you can walk to.
That is why the men who held him wanted one, and why the men who denied
the death could not use one.

slides.body: the graveyard of quraysh
What does a government gain by naming the exact ground a prisoner is buried in?

Al-Kulayni closes his notice on Musa b. Ja'far with an address. The man died in the prison of al-Sindi b. Shahik, and the government buried him in the graveyard of Quraysh at Baghdad. That is a place with a gate and a keeper, and anyone who doubted the death could walk to it in an afternoon. The compiler gives no eulogy at that point. He gives a location, and the location is the argument.

Location mattered because the alternative to a grave was a rumour. Al-Mufid records that a group had held, while Musa b. Ja'far was alive, that he would not die at all. A man with no grave suits that claim. A man with a marked plot in the Quraysh cemetery at Baghdad does not. The jailer, the caliph and the men who denied the death were all arguing about the same square of ground.

Al-Sindi understood the problem before the burial. Al-Mufid describes what he did with the body first: he brought in the jurists of Baghdad and its notable men, walked them past it, and asked what they saw. They reported no wound. They reported no mark of strangling. He wrote their testimony down. Only then did the body go out of the prison and onto the bridge.

The bridge came before the graveyard, and the order of those two things tells you the sequence of the worry. A viewing answers the question of whether the man is dead. A grave answers the question of where he is now. Al-Sindi needed both answers on the record within a day, because a body that stays inside a prison wall settles nothing for the people outside it.

Al-Kulayni also fixes the beginning. He gives the summons out of Medina on the twentieth of Shawwal in the year 179, then Basra, then Baghdad. The notice reads like a transfer file: dates, custodians, a destination. He names 'Isa b. Ja'far as the first jailer and al-Sindi b. Shahik as the last. Two men held one prisoner, and the record keeps both names.

[[NEEDS CLAIM: how many months separated the Basra custody from the Baghdad custody, al-Kafi p. 451]]. The gap matters to the arithmetic behind the figure of nineteen years, and the figure is what the running head of this essay rests on. Al-Kulayni gives one date with a day in it. Everything else in the sequence needs a second source before it can carry a number.

The graveyard of Quraysh outlived every man in the story. The quarter around it took the name of the man buried there. [[NEEDS CLAIM: when the cemetery ground became known by the name al-Kazimiyya, and on whose authority]]. Al-Kulayni, writing generations later, still names the place as a cemetery rather than as a shrine, which is a small fact about the date of his source and a large one about the city.

Al-Mufid and al-Kulayni agree on the custody and on the grave, and they differ in what they carry. Al-Kulayni gives the itinerary and stops. From al-Mufid you get the viewing, the testimony of the jurists of Baghdad, the announcement, and the crowd that came to the bridge to look at a dead man's face. Neither is patching the other. They answer two questions that one death raised a century apart.

Hold both. The itinerary explains how a man summoned out of Medina came to die inside a Baghdad prison after two custodians and one journey by way of Basra. The viewing explains why his jailer handled a corpse the way a registrar handles a document. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any early source names the men who washed and buried him at the Quraysh cemetery]]. Between the two accounts sits the grave, and the grave is where the argument landed.
The cemetery was the only part of the case that could not be argued with, which is why the state produced it and why the men who had staked everything on a living imam had to walk past it.

post.running_head: two dates and the road between them
post.caption:
Al-Kulayni gives a day, a month and a year for the summons that took Musa
b. Ja'far out of Medina. He gives no day at all for the death. One end of
the custody is dated to the afternoon. The other end is dated to a year.

slides.body: twenty shawwal
Why does the record keep the day a prisoner was taken and lose the day he arrived?

The record keeps the day the escort took him. Al-Kulayni dates the summons out of Medina to the twentieth of Shawwal in 179: a day, a month and a year, which is the precision a chancery keeps and a memory does not. He places Harun at Medina on the return from the umra in Ramadan. The caliph then went on to the hajj and took Musa b. Ja'far with him toward Basra, where the arrival is dated to no day at all.

Read that itinerary again. The prisoner travelled inside the caliph's own pilgrimage caravan. Harun did not send a squad to Medina to seize a man in the night and drag him to Iraq. He collected him on a journey the whole Hijaz could watch, and then continued to Basra, where 'Isa b. Ja'far took custody of him. The arrest wore the clothes of an escort.

Al-Mufid supplies the other end. He dates the death to the sixth of Rajab in 183 and puts it in the prison of al-Sindi b. Shahik at Baghdad. He gives the age as fifty-five. Two compilers, working from different material, between them fix a span: Shawwal 179 to Rajab 183. Everything the account has to say about custody happens inside that window.

The window runs to something under four years. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the exact interval between 20 Shawwal 179 and 6 Rajab 183 in lunar months]]. That figure sits against the phrase which follows this man through every later retelling, the one that speaks of nineteen years in custody. Both numbers cannot describe the same thing. Either the shorter one counts the final imprisonment and the longer one counts a lifetime of detentions, or somebody has added two spans that overlap. No source on this shelf states which, and the difference is the whole claim.

One count measures the last custody. The other count reaches back to earlier arrests under earlier caliphs, which is a much longer stretch and a much vaguer one. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the year of the first arrest under al-Mahdi, and who ordered it]]. Al-Kulayni preserves a report of Musa b. Ja'far being brought before al-Mahdi and halting at Zabala on the road, so the earlier detentions are not an invention of later devotion.

The difference between four years and nineteen is the difference between a case and a career. A four-year custody is a political decision by one caliph. A nineteen-year pattern is a policy held by three of them across three reigns. Anyone who repeats the larger figure is making the second claim, and the arithmetic behind it has to be shown rather than inherited.

A policy held across three reigns would leave traces in three kinds of record, and al-Kulayni's precision at the front end tells you what kind he had. A dated summons on the twentieth of Shawwal reads like a note taken from a register, or from somebody who watched the caravan leave Medina. His death notice carries no such day. Al-Mufid supplies one, working later and drawing on material that had settled inside the community by his time.

The Arabic chronicle of al-Tabari enters the death without a day at all, under the year, beside the death of the qadi Muhammad b. al-Sammak. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the full wording of al-Tabari's notice at 8:271]]. For a chronicler working by years, a prisoner's death is one line in a list. The absence of a date is not concealment. It is the shape of the genre.

So the two ends of this custody sit in different kinds of record, and the genre of a source decides what it can tell you. The beginning is administrative and dated to the day. The end reaches us twice: dated to the day by a compiler writing two centuries downstream, and dated to the year by a chronicler working from the state's own files. Choosing between those two is not possible from here. Naming which is which is.

Naming which is which leaves one job. A date pair is only as strong as the weaker of its two dates, and both of these dates rest on a single book. Shawwal 179 rests on al-Kulayni alone in the material on this shelf. Rajab 183 rests on al-Mufid alone. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any source earlier than al-Kafi carries the 20 Shawwal 179 summons]]. Until somebody checks that, the span is a claim about two compilers rather than a claim about four years.
The state wrote down the day it took him and the year it lost him, and that asymmetry is the whole administrative history of the case in two lines.

post.running_head: the prisoner who was moved twice
post.caption:
Harun did not keep Musa b. Ja'far in one place. Al-Kulayni names two
custodians in two cities: 'Isa b. Ja'far at Basra, then al-Sindi b. Shahik
at Baghdad. A state that moves a prisoner is a state that has run out of
patience with the first arrangement.

slides.body: the prison at basra
What goes wrong with a custody that makes a caliph change the jailer?

Al-Kulayni names two jailers. 'Isa b. Ja'far held Musa b. Ja'far at Basra after the hajj. Later Harun summoned the prisoner to Baghdad and handed him to al-Sindi b. Shahik. The compiler reports the move without a reason, the way a file records a transfer. Two cities, two custodians, one prisoner, and a caliph who changed his mind about where the man should sit.

Basra was no punishment posting. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the standing of Basra among the cities of Iraq in the 170s AH]]. 'Isa b. Ja'far belonged to the ruling house, and the choice of him says something the compiler does not spell out. [[NEEDS CLAIM: 'Isa b. Ja'far's office and family connection to Harun]]. Handing a prisoner to a relative in a large city keeps him comfortable and keeps him watched, and it spreads the responsibility for whatever happens next across two branches of one family.

Comfort has a cost for a jailer. A prisoner who receives visitors builds a following inside the prison, and the followers carry messages out of it. [[NEEDS CLAIM: any report of who visited Musa b. Ja'far during the Basra custody]]. The record of the later Baghdad custody shows a network still operating: money moved, agents reported, and the men holding both ends knew each other's names.

Then Harun moved him. Baghdad was the caliph's own city, and al-Sindi b. Shahik was the caliph's own man rather than a cousin with a household, a following and interests of his own to protect. The change reads as a tightening. A prisoner in Basra sits in somebody else's town, under somebody else's judgement about how much comfort is safe. A prisoner in Baghdad sits where the orders are written and where the man who wrote them can send for him before nightfall.

Al-Mufid shows how those orders arrived. Yahya b. Khalid travelled to Baghdad and told the city he had come to look into the tax administration of the Sawad. He spent a few days on the accounts. Then he sent for al-Sindi and gave him his instructions about the prisoner. The cover story was fiscal, the errand was not, and al-Mufid states both in the same breath.

A minister who travels in person carries something a letter cannot. The instruction has no seal, no copy, no clerk and no archive, which means it leaves no evidence and admits no denial later. Al-Mufid writes that the order concerned Musa b. Ja'far, and then reports what people said the order was: poison in the food, with dates named as the vehicle. He marks that part as something said rather than something known, and the mark is doing real work.

That marking is the honest part of the chapter, and it is worth pausing on. Al-Mufid could have written the poison as fact. His readers expected it, the charge was already old by his day, and nothing in his book would have been weakened by stating it flat. He wrote it as a report that reached him and left the seam showing. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the Arabic phrase al-Mufid uses to introduce the poison report, Irshad p. 427]]. A compiler who marks his own weak joints is telling you where to push.

The Arabic chronicle disagrees by silence. Al-Tabari enters the death at Baghdad under its year, beside the death of a qadi, and says nothing about a cause, a minister or an instruction. Two accounts survive. One comes from a compiler writing inside the community that mourned the man, the other from a chronicler working with the state's own year-by-year files, and only one of them has a poison in it. Silence in an annal is not a denial, and it is not a confirmation either.

Neither the silence nor the report settles the question, and a carousel that pretends otherwise is lying to a reader who has no way to check it. What the two sources do settle between them is the custody: Basra first under a kinsman of the caliph, Baghdad second under a servant of his, a transfer between the two, and a minister who arrived in the second city with instructions that nobody entered in a register. That is a good deal to know about a man held without a charge.

[[NEEDS CLAIM: how long the Basra custody lasted]]. Without that figure the transfer stays ambiguous: a caliph losing patience with a cousin, or a routine consolidation of prisoners in the capital. One number decides between those two readings. It is the single figure that would turn this essay from an argument into a demonstration, and nothing on this shelf carries it, which is why the sentence above still has brackets in it.
A caliph who trusts a custody leaves it where it is, and Harun moved this one the length of [[NEEDS CLAIM: the road distance from Basra to Baghdad]] to put it under a man with no cousins to please.

post.running_head: the road from medina to iraq
post.caption:
A man on the Kufa road remembered the night the escort stopped at his
town. Al-Kulayni kept his name and his mood: 'Ali b. Khalid al-Zabali,
depressed, watching a prisoner being taken north to al-Mahdi.

Stages on a pilgrim road are how an empire moves people. The report is a
map with one stage on it.

slides.body: the halt at zabala
How many towns does a prisoner pass through before the record loses him?

Al-Kulayni keeps one witness at one stage of the road. 'Ali b. Khalid al-Zabali says that when the escort brought Musa b. Ja'far before al-Mahdi the first time, they put the prisoner up at Zabala for the night. The two men talked. Al-Zabali admits that he was low, says so to the prisoner's face, and gets a question back: why do I see you depressed? The whole report turns on that exchange, and the town in it is a real town with a name a traveller would recognise.

Notice what that exchange assumes. A local man could reach a prisoner in state custody, sit with him and hold a conversation about his own mood. This is not a dungeon. It is a stage on a road, with a lodging, a guard detail and a town that knows who has arrived. [[NEEDS CLAIM: where Zabala lay on the Kufa road, and its distance from Kufa]].

Roads in this account are not scenery. Al-Kulayni's other notice moves the same man from Medina to Basra to Baghdad, and the movement is the story: each stage hands him to different men. A prisoner who travels is a prisoner whose supporters know where he is on a given week. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the stages named between Medina and Basra in any source on this shelf]].

Al-Zabali's report belongs to an earlier arrest rather than to the last one. He names al-Mahdi, not Harun. That puts the halt at Zabala at least one caliph before the death in the prison of al-Sindi b. Shahik, and it means the road carried this prisoner more than once. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the year of the summons under al-Mahdi]]. Two summonses, two escorts, two sets of guards paid out of the treasury, and one direction of travel.

Direction is the argument. Medina held the family, the property and the followers who arrived every year with the pilgrimage. Iraq held the caliph, the army and the treasury. Every summons in this record runs the same way, out of the Hijaz and into Iraq, and no source on this shelf reports a caliph making the journey in reverse to hold the conversation in Medina. Power did not travel. The prisoner did.

A pilgrim road already had the infrastructure that a prisoner transfer needs. Wells, staging posts and towns that fed travellers. [[NEEDS CLAIM: who built and maintained the stages on the Kufa road, and when]]. The state did not build a special apparatus to move this man. It used the one the pilgrimage had paid for, which is why a local man at Zabala could walk up and talk to him.

That is also why an escort leaks. Al-Zabali remembered a night and a conversation. Somebody wrote his account down, it passed through a chain of transmitters whose names al-Kulayni keeps, and it landed in a chapter about authority two centuries later. A closed prison produces silence. A road produces witnesses, and witnesses on a road are most of what the later compilers had to work from.

Geography also decides what a following can do. A network with agents in Kufa and in Baghdad sits on the same road the escort used, drinks at the same wells and pays the same guides. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the towns where Musa b. Ja'far's agents are named in al-Kafi]]. Money and messages moved along the route the prisoner moved along, in both directions, which is why a transfer that looks like isolation on a map was nothing of the kind on the ground.

The last journey ran through Basra and ended in Baghdad. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any source describes the route from Basra to Baghdad taken with the prisoner]]. Al-Kulayni gives cities and custodians for that leg and no stages at all. Compare the two passages and you can see two kinds of source: a man who was standing in Zabala that night, and a clerk's note listing where a prisoner was held. Both are worth having, and only one of them has weather in it.

A map post is only as good as its stages, and this route has one halt on it that a source will support, no more than that. Zabala. One night, one conversation, one local man who was sorry to see the escort arrive. Everything else here is a line drawn between two city names, and a line drawn between two city names is a guess holding a ruler. Say that on the slide. The alternative is a map that claims more than the sources gave you, which is the standard way this format lies.
The empire moved its most awkward prisoner along the road it had built for pilgrims, and that is why we know the name of a man in Zabala who was sorry to see him pass.

post.running_head: the arithmetic of a succession
post.caption:
Al-Mufid lists the children of Musa b. Ja'far by name: thirty-seven, sons
and daughters, with the mothers marked. A household that size is not a
family detail. It is the size of the problem the succession had to solve.

slides.body: thirty-seven names
What happens to a claim of authority when the man who holds it leaves thirty-seven heirs?

Al-Mufid does not summarise the household. He lists it. Thirty-seven children of Musa b. Ja'far, sons and daughters, set out by name with the mothers marked beside them. The list runs from 'Ali b. Musa al-Rida at the head down through Umm Kulthum at the foot. A compiler who wanted a symbolic number would not have written out thirty-seven of them.

Count the arithmetic the list forces. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the split between sons and daughters in al-Mufid's list, Irshad pp. 428-429]]. Every son in it is a possible claimant, a possible rallying point and a standing expense. The succession did not have to beat one rival. It had to settle a room, and the room was large enough that the compiler needed two pages to name everyone in it.

Al-Mufid resolves it in a sentence. The most outstanding of the children, he writes, the greatest in rank and the most learned, was 'Ali b. Musa al-Rida. That is a judgement rather than a document, and he offers it where a list would otherwise leave a reader to choose. The compiler is steering, and he does it in the open.

Ahmad b. Musa gets the next paragraph, and it is a paragraph about property. His father gave him the estate known as al-Yasira. He is said to have freed a thousand slaves. A man who can free a thousand slaves is a man with an income, and the report attaches that income to a brother who did not inherit the office.

A thousand is the kind of number that grows in the telling, and al-Mufid hands it over with the words it is said. [[NEEDS CLAIM: any second source for the thousand freed slaves, or for the estate of al-Yasira]]. Take the figure as a claim about scale rather than as a count, and the point still stands: the household held land, and the land produced enough to matter.

Land, brothers, and a following spread across Iraq and the Hijaz give you the shape of the inheritance dispute. The office went one way. The money did not have to follow it, and in a community where agents collected in the name of an imam, the two could come apart without anyone announcing a split. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the sources say about the property of Musa b. Ja'far at the time of his death]]. Property is the part of a succession that leaves receipts.

This is where the number stops being trivia. A group among the followers held that Musa b. Ja'far had not died at all, and men in that group had custody of funds collected in his name across Iraq and the Hijaz. Thirty-seven heirs and an undivided treasury make a standing argument on their own. Add a doctrine which says the owner is alive and will return, and the argument acquires a reason never to close.

Al-Mufid writes the list before he writes the dispute, and that order is a choice. His reader meets the household first, counts how many people the estate had to satisfy, and only then hears that part of the following refused the successor. Put the dispute first and it reads as doctrine. Put the household first and it reads as an inheritance case with doctrine attached. The compiler is making an argument with his table of contents.

Set the numbers side by side and the essay has its shape. 37 children, 1 designated successor, and a life that runs 128 AH to 183 AH, which is 55 years by the count al-Mufid gives on his own page 407. Set 37 against 55 and the household stops looking like a footnote to the biography and starts looking like the institution the biography is about. [[NEEDS CLAIM: how many of the thirty-seven are reported to have made a claim of their own, and in which sources]]. Even one such claim changes what the community argued about after Rajab 183.

The list also fixes the social record. Al-Mufid marks the mothers of these children as slave-wives, without apology and without embellishment, in the middle of a book written to establish authority. He expected no reader to flinch. A reader in 2026 flinches, and the honest move is to report what the page says, name the gap between his century and this one, and let the difference stand where the reader can see it.
A succession that has to be argued for is a succession with competition in the house, and al-Mufid gave the competition names, thirty-seven of them, before he told you who won.

post.running_head: a date in the middle of a quiet month
post.caption:
Al-Mufid gives the death of Musa b. Ja'far a day: the sixth of Rajab, 183.
Rajab is one of the months in which fighting was forbidden. The date sits
in the calendar's quietest quarter, and the prison it names was in the
capital.

slides.body: six rajab
What does a community do with a death that has a date but no ceremony?

Al-Mufid fixes the death to a day. The sixth of Rajab, in the year 183, inside the prison of al-Sindi b. Shahik at Baghdad. He gives the age as fifty-five and the length of the Imamate as thirty-five years. Four figures in two sentences. A compiler who wanted a legend would have written a scene; this one wrote a register entry, and the entry is what the calendar has been built on ever since.

A day in the calendar does work that a year cannot. A year is history. A day comes round again. Once the sixth of Rajab has a name attached, every Rajab afterwards carries an appointment, and the community that keeps it does not need a shrine, a state or a permission to keep it. It needs a date and a memory of what the date holds.

That is why this account runs a mourning setting at all. From Muharram 1 to Safar 30 the covers go solid, the ground goes dark, the ornament comes off, and the ink drops to bone on near black. The wafat dates do the same thing for a single day. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the wafat dates as published in Sistani's calendar, month and day]]. Those dates are a religious determination, so a machine does not get to guess them.

The tooling in this repository holds that line. It converts a Gregorian date to a Hijri date by arithmetic, reports the answer, and says out loud that a sighted calendar can differ from the tabular one by a day. Near a boundary it refuses to decide and tells the operator to check the published calendar. A pipeline that flipped a design token on its own would put ornament on a mourning morning inside a year.

Rajab itself carries a rule older than the dispute in this story. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the four months in which fighting was forbidden, and the source that lists them]]. A death in a prison during such a month has a shape that a death in any other month does not, and the sources that report it were writing for readers who felt that shape without being told.

A modern reader does not feel it, which is a problem this account has to solve on the slide rather than in a footnote. Name the month. Say what the month meant. Give the reader the calendar the way you would give a stranger a map, and do not assume that the word Rajab is doing any work in their head before you put it there.

The other half of the calendar problem is the burial. Al-Kulayni names the graveyard of Quraysh at Baghdad and stops. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any early source gives the day of the burial rather than the day of the death]]. A death has a date in this record. A funeral does not, and the men who ran the funeral were the men who ran the prison.

Consider what that means for a family in Medina. News travelled the road the prisoner had travelled, at the speed of a caravan. [[NEEDS CLAIM: how long a message took from Baghdad to Medina in this period]]. By the time the household heard the date, the sixth of Rajab was weeks behind them, and the first mourning any of them kept was already an anniversary rather than a funeral.

That gap between the death and the news is where the dispute got its air. Al-Mufid reports that the jailer put the body on the bridge at Baghdad and called the city to look at the face. Baghdad saw. Medina heard, later, from travellers. A community which learns of a death by report rather than by sight is a community in which a denial of the death costs nothing to hold.

So the calendar carries two things at once. It carries a date fixed to the day by a compiler working from Imami material, and it carries the memory of an argument about whether the day happened. Both survive in the same chapter of the same book. Keeping the second one visible is the difference between a commemoration and an account.
A community that could not attend the funeral kept the date instead, and the date has outlasted the prison, the bridge and the men who arranged the viewing.

post.running_head: the jurists who were asked to look
post.caption:
Al-Sindi b. Shahik did not ask the jurists of Baghdad whether the prisoner
had been poisoned. He asked them whether they could see a wound. They
could not, and they said so, and he wrote it down. The question you are
asked decides the answer you can give.

slides.body: no mark upon him
Which question did the jailer put to the men he called in to see the body?

Al-Mufid names the procedure. Al-Sindi b. Shahik brought the jurists of Baghdad and its notable men into the prison, al-Haytham b. 'Adi among them, and walked them past the body. They looked. They found no wound on it and no mark of strangling. Al-Sindi then had them testify that the man had died a normal death, and they gave that testimony, and the record of it went into the account al-Mufid was reading two centuries later.

Read the finding and the testimony side by side, because they are not the same statement. The finding is narrow: no wound, no ligature. The testimony is wide: a normal death. Between those two sentences sits every method of killing a man that leaves no mark, and the men who signed had no way to rule any of them out by looking at a face.

That gap is not al-Mufid's invention. He reports the finding first and the testimony second, in that order, which lets a careful reader see the join between them. A compiler smoothing the story would have written that the jurists of Baghdad confirmed a natural death, and stopped there, and no reader a thousand years later would have known what the men had been shown or what they were asked. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether al-Mufid names any jurist who declined to testify]].

Al-Haytham b. 'Adi is the one name he keeps out of the whole delegation. [[NEEDS CLAIM: who al-Haytham b. 'Adi was, his dates and his standing as a transmitter]]. A jailer collecting testimony picks witnesses whose word carries weight in the city he has to convince, and the pick is part of the procedure. Naming even one of them tells you what the exercise was for. Testimony meant to sit in a file needs no famous signature. Testimony meant to be quoted in an argument needs several.

The design shows in what he did next. Al-Sindi took the body out of the prison, set it down on the bridge at Baghdad, and had an announcement made: this man has died, come and look at him. Testimony from named jurists reaches the men who read and who write. A body on a bridge reaches everybody else in the city, including the illiterate and the hostile. He ran both channels inside a day.

A jailer with something to hide does neither of those things. He buries at night, says little, and lets the rumour run, because a rumour with no body attached to it fades inside a season. Al-Sindi ran hard in the opposite direction on both channels within a day. What he feared was not a charge of murder, which no viewing could have answered. He feared a claim that there was no corpse at all, and a viewing answers that.

Al-Mufid supports that reading in the same paragraph. He writes that a group had claimed, during the life of Musa b. Ja'far, that he was the awaited one who would hold the office for the rest of time. The viewing answers that claim. It does not answer the question of poison, and nothing al-Sindi arranged that day was built to answer it.

The poison enters the account through a different door. Al-Mufid reports it as something said: that the instruction came through Yahya b. Khalid, that the poison went into food, that dates carried it, that a fever held three days. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the wording that introduces the three-day fever, Irshad p. 427]]. He marks it. The Arabic chronicle of al-Tabari carries no cause at all, and two accounts that differ this way have to be named as two.

So the testimony proves less than it was collected to prove and more than a sceptic allows. It does not establish a natural death. It establishes that a body existed, that named men of Baghdad filed past it, and that the state wanted their names attached to what they had seen with their own eyes. For the argument running in the city that week, that was the whole case, and the state won it.

[[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any source records what the Waqifa said about the viewing on the bridge]]. That is the missing witness statement in this case, and its absence shapes everything above. The men who denied the death had to account for a corpse that a crowd walked past in daylight. How they did it, and whether they tried, would settle what kind of movement they were: a faction with a case, or a position that nobody could withdraw from without losing everything.
Al-Sindi asked a question that could be answered by looking, got his answer in writing, and left the question that mattered to a reader standing on the bridge with no way to check it.

post.running_head: the last instruction a prisoner gave
post.caption:
Al-Sindi b. Shahik offered to shroud the body. Musa b. Ja'far refused him
and named a retainer of his own household to do the washing instead. The
refusal is recorded in the jailer's own voice, which is the strangest
thing about it.

slides.body: the shroud he refused
Why would a jailer preserve the story of a prisoner turning down his favour?

Al-Mufid keeps the exchange in al-Sindi's own words. The jailer asked for permission to shroud the body and the prisoner refused him. Musa b. Ja'far told him that the dowries of the women of the household, the pilgrimages performed on behalf of its dead, and the shrouding of its dead could be handled by a retainer of the house and by nobody else. He named the man. Al-Sindi says he did as he was asked.

Take the report at the level of procedure first. A prisoner in state custody issued an instruction about his own corpse, and the officer holding him carried it out. That is not the behaviour of a man disposing of an inconvenience. It is the behaviour of an official who knows that the household will inspect what he did and that his own name will be attached to the answer.

Now take it as a source. The report reaches al-Mufid through al-Sindi. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the chain by which al-Sindi's account of the refusal was transmitted, Irshad p. 428]]. A story that makes the jailer look punctilious travels well in the jailer's own circle, and a story that shows the prisoner giving orders travels well in the other camp. This one served both, which is a decent reason for its survival.

The content of the refusal is a rule about purity and about who belongs to a house. Musa b. Ja'far did not say that al-Sindi was unfit as a man. He said that a member of the family is washed by a retainer of the family. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the fiqh rule on who may wash and shroud the dead, and the earliest source for it]].

A rule of that kind draws a line that a state cannot cross by force. The caliph could move this man from Medina to Basra to Baghdad, could hold him without a charge and could hand him from one custodian to another. He could not make his officer the person who prepared the body. The last jurisdiction left to a prisoner was three feet wide, and he used it.

The refusal also carries an expectation. A man who names the retainer who will wash him expects to be washed, buried and mourned in the ordinary way. He is not arranging for a disappearance or for a return. Against the claim that this imam would not die at all, the instruction is evidence from the only witness who could not be accused of guessing.

Nobody in the later argument seems to have used it that way, and the silence is worth a slide of its own. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any source cites the shroud instruction against the Waqifa]]. The controversy ran on lists of transmitters, on chains and on doctrine. This small procedural detail sat in the record with nobody reaching for it, which suggests the two sides were not arguing about evidence in the way a modern reader assumes they were.

Al-Mufid places the passage after the viewing on the bridge and before the list of the thirty-seven children. Death, then proof of death, then the household that has to carry on. The chapter is arranged like a case file rather than like a life, and the shroud instruction is the document that closes the section on the body. What follows it is inheritance, and the compiler moves from one to the other without a paragraph of grief between them.

Compare the Arabic chronicle one more time. Al-Tabari has the death, the city and the year, and carries nothing about a shroud, a retainer or a refusal, because none of that belongs in an annal. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any chronicle outside the Imami tradition records the burial arrangements]]. The detail survives because a community kept it, and a community keeps what it can use. Ask what this one was using it for and the answer is continuity.

What they used it for was continuity. A retainer of the house washed the body, the house buried him in the graveyard of Quraysh, and the house went on with 'Ali b. Musa al-Rida at its head. Each of those is an administrative fact before it is anything else, and the chain of them is what a succession looks like from the outside.
The last order this prisoner gave was about a piece of cloth, and the officer who had spent months holding him obeyed it.

post.running_head: the men who stopped at the eighth name
post.caption:
Al-Kulayni's chains carry a label: this transmitter belonged to the
Waqifa, the men who stopped at Musa b. Ja'far and refused the son. The
compiler kept the label and kept the report. That decision tells you what
a chain of transmission was for.

slides.body: the ones who halted
Why does a compiler keep a report from a man he says belonged to the wrong party?

Open al-Kafi at the chains. The label sits in the middle of them. Marwan al-Qandi, from the Waqifa, who said the following. Al-Wasiti, a member of the Waqifa, who said the following. Al-Kulayni neither drops these men from his book nor hides what they were, and he had every reason to do one or the other. He writes the party name into the chain, hands over the report, and leaves the weighing to whoever is reading.

The label names a position rather than a personality. The Waqifa stopped at Musa b. Ja'far. They held that the man who died in the prison of al-Sindi b. Shahik had not died, or would return, and they refused the succession of his son. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the earliest source that uses the name Waqifa, and what it says the group held]].

Al-Mufid shows the position forming before the death rather than after it. He writes that a group had claimed, while Musa b. Ja'far was alive, that he was the awaited one who would hold the office for the rest of time. A doctrine that predates the corpse cannot be explained as grief. It was a reading of what the imamate was, and the death tested it in public.

The test happened on a bridge. Al-Sindi displayed the body and called Baghdad to look at the face, and al-Mufid states that the group's claim is why he did it. A movement that survives that is a movement with an answer ready, and the answer had to be either that the body was not his or that a return was still coming.

[[NEEDS CLAIM: what the Waqifa are reported to have said in reply to the viewing]]. Without that, this essay can describe the state's move and not the reply to it, which is half a controversy. The reply is the piece that would show whether these men were a faction with a case or a group holding a position that had already failed.

Money is the part of the story the sources do not hide. Agents collected in the name of an imam, and men holding funds when he died had a decision to make about whom to hand them to. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the sources say about funds held by agents at the death of Musa b. Ja'far]]. A doctrine that keeps the previous imam alive also keeps the accounts where they are.

That is an accusation later writers made, and it needs naming as an accusation rather than as a finding. [[NEEDS CLAIM: which source first attributes the Waqifa position to the retention of funds]]. A charge of self-interest is easy to write and hard to check, and this account does not repeat a charge whose earliest source it has not read.

What can be checked is that men left. Al-Kulayni preserves a transmitter saying that he came to Khurasan while he belonged to the Waqifa, which is a sentence about a change of mind. Khurasan is where 'Ali b. Musa al-Rida later stood at the centre of a much larger political story. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the date of that report and the page in al-Kafi]].

Now the compiler's decision looks less like tolerance and more like method. A chain exists so that a reader can weigh a report by the men who carried it. Erasing the label would make the report look stronger than it is. Keeping it lets a later reader discount the report, accept it, or notice that a man who once denied the succession is the one carrying it.

The dispute outlived everyone who started it. Al-Kulayni compiled his book generations after the death in the prison, and he still needed the word in his chains. That means readers in his own day still met men who held the position, or books that came out of it, or reports whose weight depended on knowing where the transmitter had stood. [[NEEDS CLAIM: how long the Waqifa persisted as a distinct group, and the source]].
The party that stopped at the eighth name kept its place in the record as a label attached to men whose reports the other side went on quoting.

post.running_head: the household behind the office
post.caption:
Al-Mufid names the mother of Musa b. Ja'far in the same sentence as the
date of his birth: a slave-wife, Hamida al-Barbariyya. Al-Kulayni names
her too, and carries a report about how she entered the household. The
sources are franker about this than their later readers are.

slides.body: a slave-wife called hamida
Who was in the room when the succession that mattered was arranged?

Al-Mufid writes the birth and the mother in one breath. Musa b. Ja'far was born at al-Abwa' in the year 128, and his mother was a slave-wife named Hamida al-Barbariyya. Al-Kulayni gives the same fact in his own notice, with the term umm walad, and adds the name Hamida. Two independent compilers, two vocabularies, one woman, and neither of them treats her status as something to be managed.

The nisba attached to her name points somewhere, and the sources do not say where. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what al-Barbariyya indicates about Hamida's origin, and the earliest source for it]]. A household at Medina in the 120s drew people out of slave markets that reached from the Atlantic coast of Africa to the Oxus. Her name preserves a trace of that traffic and withholds the road she came by, the price paid, and the age she was when somebody paid it.

Al-Kulayni goes further than the label. He carries a report in which Ja'far b. Muhammad is told to take her, and a saying that Hamida is clean of uncleanness in the way purified gold is clean. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the full text and page of the Hamida report in al-Kafi]]. That is a defence, and the presence of a defence tells you that somebody had made an attack.

The attack is easy to reconstruct in outline and impossible to source from this shelf. An office passing from father to son runs into a question about the mothers of the sons the moment a rival wants one asked. Standing, in that world, came down through women as well as men. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any source records an objection to Musa b. Ja'far's succession on the grounds of his mother's status]]. Until such a row is found, the defence in al-Kafi is the only evidence that an attack existed.

Al-Mufid answers the question a different way, by not raising it. He states the status in the biographical opening, moves to the designation reports, and lets seven named companions of the father carry the case for the son. A compiler who thought the mother's status was a weakness would not have put it in the second paragraph of the chapter.

Read the list of thirty-seven children and the pattern repeats. Al-Mufid marks group after group of them with the same phrase: their mothers were slave-wives. He is describing the ordinary arrangement of a large household in that society, and he expects no reader to be surprised. A modern reader is surprised, and the surprise is a fact about the reader.

This account does not soften that and does not celebrate it. The women in these households were unfree. Their sons inherited standing, property and in one case an office that a community still argues about. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what legal status an umm walad held in this period, and the source that sets it out]]. Both things are true at once and the slide has room for both.

That structure is worth naming for anybody reading a biographical notice for the first time. It is a form rather than a narrative, and the form decides what survives the centuries. A woman who bore an imam gets a name and a phrase. A jailer gets a name and a city. A brother gets a line about an estate. Everything a modern reader wants to know about any of them falls outside the fields the form allows, and no amount of rereading will put it back.

So the honest fact panel here is short. A woman called Hamida, of a status the sources name without euphemism, mother of a man born at al-Abwa' in 128 who died in a Baghdad prison in 183. Around that stand two reports defending her against something the sources never quote, and a household of thirty-seven children whose mothers are marked the same way. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether Hamida outlived her son]]. That last question has an answer somewhere, and this account does not have it.
The chapter that argues hardest for a man's authority opens by telling you his mother was owned, and the compiler saw no tension there at all.

post.running_head: seven men who said they were told
post.cover_title: the boy asleep in the room
post.caption:
Al-Mufid lists the men who reported that Ja'far b. Muhammad designated his
son Musa: al-Mufaddal b. 'Umar, Mu'adh b. Kathir, 'Abd al-Rahman b.
al-Hajjaj, al-Fayd b. al-Mukhtar, Ya'qub al-Sarraj, Sulayman b. Khalid,
Safwan al-Jammal. Names, not atmosphere.

slides.body: the boy asleep in the room
How do you prove a private conversation happened sixty years after everyone in it died?

Al-Mufid answers the private conversation problem by naming names. He lists the shaykhs of the father's circle who reported the designation of the son: al-Mufaddal b. 'Umar al-Ju'fi, Mu'adh b. Kathir, 'Abd al-Rahman b. al-Hajjaj, al-Fayd b. al-Mukhtar, Ya'qub al-Sarraj, Sulayman b. Khalid, Safwan al-Jammal. Then he adds that two of the son's own brothers, Ishaq and 'Ali, reported it as well, and says the full list would make the book too long.

Count what that list is doing. It is not a chain of transmission from one man. It is a claim of independent multiple attestation, made in the vocabulary a tenth-century reader would test it in. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether these seven appear in the standard biographical dictionaries, and how they are graded there]]. Al-Mufid is inviting the check, which is a strong move to make if the names cannot survive it.

The reports behind those names are small domestic scenes rather than ceremonies. Al-Mufaddal is sitting with the father when the boy comes in, and the father tells him to indicate to the companions he trusts that authority belongs to this child. Mu'adh b. Kathir asks for a successor and gets a hand pointing at a sleeping boy. Nothing in either scene happens in public, and nothing in either would leave a document behind.

That privacy is the whole problem and the whole point. A designation made in front of a crowd would have been contested by the crowd and by every faction standing in it. A designation made to trusted men, one at a time, in a room, produces the record in front of us: al-Mufaddal, Mu'adh and the rest, each saying he was told, with no paper of any kind behind them. A compiler two centuries later counts the men because he has no document to count.

'Abd al-Rahman b. al-Hajjaj, third on that list of men, gives the line that stays with a reader. He asks the father who the master of the affair will be, and the father tells him that Musa has put on the armour and it fitted him. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the Arabic of that phrase and its idiomatic force]]. The metaphor says fit rather than blood. It claims the son suits the office, which is a different argument from saying he is next in line.

Al-Fayd b. al-Mukhtar asks in the bluntest terms in the set. Take my hand away from the fire, he says, who is the imam for us after you? The boy walks in and the father tells him: this is your leader, keep close to him. A follower asking about salvation gets an answer about a specific child in a specific room.

Al-Mufid footnotes the lot of them to al-Kafi and says that al-Kulayni's chains have been shortened. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the al-Kafi volume, page and tradition numbers al-Mufid cites for these reports]]. A compiler who shortens a chain and tells you he has shortened it is handing you the means to go behind him, which is the opposite of what a fabricator does.

Against all of that sits an awkward fact. This evidence convinced part of the following and not the rest. The Waqifa refused the son and stopped at the father, which means seven named men and two brothers failed to settle the question for everybody who heard them. Evidence is not agreement. This account will not pretend the list closed an argument that ran on for generations after the men in it were dead.

[[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any early source records a rival designation report naming a different son]]. That check matters more than any other in this file, and it bears on the refusal described on the slide before this one. A succession dispute in which both sides hold designation reports looks nothing like a dispute in which one side has reports and the other has a doctrine about a man who cannot die. The difference decides how the whole essay should be written.

One more thing about the list is worth a slide. Safwan al-Jammal carries a cameleer's trade name and Ya'qub al-Sarraj a saddler's. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the trade names of these transmitters indicate about their occupations]]. The men who carried the claim were not courtiers or judges. They were tradesmen who moved between Kufa and Medina with the caravans, and the claim travelled the way they did, at the speed of a camel, in the same season as the pilgrimage.
A private word in a room in Medina had to be carried by saddlers and cameleers, and it reached us because al-Mufid wrote down which of them said what.

post.running_head: what a caliph learns from a receipt
post.caption:
A man carried property from Khurasan to the family at Medina and asked
each recipient for a receipt. Al-Kulayni keeps the story because of what
happened when he reached Ja'far b. Muhammad, who refused, and told him
what he had been sent to do.

slides.body: the money from khurasan
What is a government buying when it hands out money and asks for a signature?

Al-Kulayni tells the receipt story from the messenger's side, which is the side that knows what the errand was. The man is given property and a script: tell them your Shi'a in Khurasan sent this to be delivered to you. Hand it over on the stated conditions. Then, as a messenger does, ask each recipient for a receipt naming the amount and the kind of property received. He goes to Medina, works through the list, and comes back with the paper.

Read the receipt as an instrument rather than as a courtesy. A signed acknowledgement that a man took money sent by the followers of his house is a document with two uses. It proves he has followers who send money. It proves he accepted it. Either fact, produced later in front of a caliph, answers a question that the man himself would rather leave open.

Running a trap like that is cheap, which is the third thing to notice about the receipt. It costs the treasury a sum nobody will miss. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the amount of property described in the report, al-Kafi p. 450]]. It buys a file of signatures from the leading men of a family the state already watches, and it buys them without an arrest, a raid, or a single accusation that anybody would afterwards have to prove in front of a judge.

One man refused. Al-Kulayni has the messenger say that everyone on the list gave him a receipt in his own hand except Ja'far b. Muhammad. He found him praying in the mosque of the Messenger, sat down behind him to wait, and got a warning before he could deliver his line: fear God, and do not deceive the family of Muhammad.

Then comes the detail the report is built for. The messenger says that the man brought his head close and told him everything that had passed between him and the caliph, as though he had been a third person in the room. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the identity of the ruler called abu al-Dawaniq in this report]]. A modern reader will take that as a claim about knowledge. Take it first as a claim about what the family already understood.

Because the refusal makes sense with no special knowledge at all. A household under surveillance learns to read an offer. Property arriving from a distant province, with a script attached, carried by a man who wants the transaction in writing, is not charity. It is an invitation to sign something. The other recipients on the list signed, took the goods and thought no more about it. One man did not, and al-Kulayni's report keeps the difference between them.

Set the story beside the custody of the next generation and the shape repeats. Al-Kulayni reports Harun summoning Musa b. Ja'far out of Medina on the twentieth of Shawwal in 179, taking him to Basra, then on to Baghdad and the prison of al-Sindi b. Shahik. Paper first, then a prison. The state tried to document a network before it tried to hold the man at the centre of it, and both attempts leave the same kind of trace.

A network is the right word for what the state was after here. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the sources say about agents collecting funds for the family in this period, and where they operated]]. Money moving from Khurasan to Medina implies people at both ends, a route between them, an understanding about rates and conditions, and a habit old enough and regular enough to be worth imitating in a forgery. Forgeries copy what already exists.

That last point matters for the essay about the Waqifa. A movement that later refused to accept a death was a movement with funds in its hands and agents in several provinces, and it did not build that apparatus in a month. This report shows the same machinery working two generations earlier. It also shows a caliph who knew the machinery existed and wanted its paperwork rather than its money.

[[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any source outside al-Kafi carries the Khurasan receipt story]]. Without a second witness this remains one community's account of its own founder outwitting a caliph, and that is a genre with a strong motive and a long history. What keeps it interesting is the administrative furniture: the script, the stated conditions, the signature, the file taken back to a ruler who asked what was left behind.
The state wanted a signature more than it wanted the money back, and the one man who understood that is the reason the story was worth keeping.

post.running_head: one life measured three ways
post.caption:
128 AH to 183 AH is 55 years. Al-Mufid gives all three numbers on one
page, and gives a fourth: 35 years of the Imamate. Subtract and the
arithmetic says something the page never states.

slides.body: fifty-five years
What do the numbers on one page of al-Mufid add up to when you subtract them?

Al-Mufid puts four numbers in a single paragraph. Birth at al-Abwa' in 128. Death on 6 Rajab 183. Age fifty-five. Imamate thirty-five years. He states them and moves on to the designation reports without drawing a conclusion from any of them. The arithmetic is left on the page for a reader to do, and doing it is the point of this post.

Start with the span itself. 183 minus 128 is 55, which matches the age al-Mufid gives, so his two figures agree and neither contradicts the other. That agreement is worth stating because it is not guaranteed anywhere. Biographical notices carry inherited numbers, inherited numbers drift as they are copied, and a compiler who never checks can print a birth year and an age that cannot both be true. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any source gives a different age at death]].

Now the second subtraction. 55 minus 35 is 20, so on al-Mufid's own figures the office came to him at about the age of twenty. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the year of Ja'far b. Muhammad's death, and the source]]. A man of twenty inheriting a following spread across two provinces is a different story from a mature scholar inheriting one, and the page never says which.

The figure of twenty sets the designation reports in a frame. Al-Mufid has the father pointing at a child asleep in a room, and at a boy walking through a door. Those scenes happen years before the office changes hands. The community had been told who was next, and then it waited. That wait is what made the answer stick when the day came, and it is also what gave a rival reading of the office time to form and to find men willing to hold it.

Third subtraction. Al-Kulayni dates the summons out of Medina to 20 Shawwal 179, and al-Mufid dates the death to Rajab 183, so the last custody runs a little under four years. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the interval between 20 Shawwal 179 and 6 Rajab 183 in lunar months]]. Four years out of thirty-five in office, which leaves thirty-one years unaccounted for by that particular imprisonment.

This is where the number card earns its keep, and where most retellings of this life go quiet. The phrase that follows Musa b. Ja'far everywhere speaks of nineteen years in custody. Nineteen does not come out of any subtraction on al-Mufid's page. It has to be assembled from arrests under more than one caliph, and the assembly needs sources this shelf does not hold.

[[NEEDS CLAIM: the years and durations of the earlier detentions under al-Mansur and al-Mahdi, with sources]]. Until rows like those exist and somebody has verified them against a printed page, the honest version of the running head at the top of this slide is a question and not a headline. This account prints headlines it can defend to a stranger who owes the tradition nothing. It does not print figures it inherited from other people's captions.

One anchor for the earlier arrests survives the test. Al-Kulayni carries a report from 'Ali b. Khalid al-Zabali, who says the escort halted at Zabala when Musa b. Ja'far was brought before al-Mahdi the first time. Read the words the first time again. They carry the weight of the sentence: they place at least one detention a full caliph before Harun, and they assume a second one that al-Zabali expected his hearers to know about without being told.

Numbers in a biography come in two kinds, and this page has both sitting side by side. The dates and the age are the kind a compiler copies out of a written notice that somebody kept at the time. The thirty-five years of Imamate is the kind a community computes for itself, from a doctrine about the moment authority passes from one man to the next. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether the thirty-five-year figure appears in any source before al-Mufid]].

A number card states its arithmetic and the two dates the arithmetic spans, and the two dates here are 128 AH and 183 AH. Everything else on this slide is subtraction from those: 55 years alive, 35 of them in office, about 20 before the office came to him, and under 4 in the final prison at Baghdad. Four operations, one page of one book, and one famous figure that the page cannot produce by any of them.
The famous number attached to this life is the one number al-Mufid's page does not contain, and nobody who repeats it says where they got it.

post.running_head: an annal has room for one line
post.caption:
The Arabic al-Tabari records the death of Musa b. Ja'far at Baghdad in its
year, beside the death of a qadi. No prison. No poison. No minister. The
silence is not a cover-up; it is what an annal is.

slides.body: what the chronicle leaves out
What does it mean when the biggest chronicle in the language gives a death one line?

The Arabic text of al-Tabari enters the death under its year. Musa b. Ja'far b. Muhammad died at Baghdad, and Muhammad b. al-Sammak the qadi died, and the year moves on. That is the whole notice on the page as this pipeline found it. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the full sentence and its immediate context at 8:271]]. One line, two men, no cause given for either.

Al-Mufid, working inside the community that kept the memory, gives the same death a chapter of its own. The prison of al-Sindi b. Shahik. The instruction carried to Baghdad by Yahya b. Khalid under cover of a tax inspection of the Sawad. The poison reported rather than asserted. The jurists of the city walked past the body and asked what they could see. The announcement on the bridge. The shroud the prisoner refused.

Two accounts of one death, and the temptation is to treat the shorter one as suppression. Resist it. An annal arranged by year is a form with fixed slots: campaigns, appointments, deaths, prices, the pilgrimage leader. A man who died in a prison gets the same line as a qadi who died in his bed, because the form does not have a field for how.

The form also decides who gets in at all. Being entered in that year's deaths means the chronicler's sources treated this man as a person of note in Baghdad. [[NEEDS CLAIM: which other deaths al-Tabari lists in the same year notice]]. The company a name keeps in an annal is a rough measure of how the capital ranked him at the time.

Where the two sources can be compared, they do not contradict each other. Both put the death at Baghdad. Both put it in the same year. Neither says the man returned home, escaped his escort, or vanished out of a locked room. On the one fact that the Waqifa denied, an Imami compiler and a chronicler working from state material agree, and they agree while sharing no obvious source between them.

That agreement is the strongest evidence in this whole file, and it arrives from the source with the least to gain by giving it. A chronicler compiling year by year in Baghdad had no stake in whether a Medinan claimant died in custody or lived on in hiding. The line cost him nothing, served no faction, and settled nothing he cared about. He wrote it, and it says died at Baghdad.

Now the harder half of the comparison. On the cause of death the two sources part company, and no amount of rereading will close the gap between them. Al-Mufid reports a poison and marks the report as something said rather than something known. Al-Tabari offers nothing at all. A slide that tells a reader the man was poisoned has chosen one source over the other and hidden the choice.

This account names both instead. Al-Mufid reports the poison as something said. The Arabic chronicle records the death with no cause attached. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether the SUNY translation of the relevant volume carries any additional notice, once a copy is registered]]. Naming both is slower to read, it fits a slide with less grace, and it is the only version a stranger has any reason to trust.

The annal has a reason to stay thin here beyond the shape of its genre. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what al-Tabari's own sources were for the years around 183]]. A chronicler compiling from official material inherits the state's silences along with the state's dates. The office that produced those records had already staged a public viewing, and a viewing is what a government does when it intends to be asked nothing further.

So the silence has a shape, and the shape is worth describing. It is not the absence of a record, and it is not a page torn out. It is a record produced by an administration which had already answered, in public, on a bridge, in front of named witnesses, the only question it meant to answer. Everything else about that death was somebody else's business to write down.
The chronicle gives this death one line and gives a judge the same line, and reading that as concealment says more about us than about the man who wrote it.

post.running_head: a man with five names in one paragraph
post.caption:
Abu Ibrahim. Abu al-Hasan. Abu 'Ali. Al-'Abd al-Salih. Al-Kazim. Al-Mufid
lists them in a single paragraph, and each one comes from a different set
of people with a different reason for using it.

slides.body: the restrained one
Why does one man need five names inside a single paragraph?

Al-Mufid sets the names out without explaining any of them. The kunyas were Abu Ibrahim, Abu al-Hasan and Abu 'Ali. He is known as al-'Abd al-Salih, the worshipper who serves. He is described as al-Kazim, the restrained. Five ways of naming one man, offered in the same paragraph as his age and the length of his Imamate, as though the count of names were one more biographical measurement alongside the years.

In one sense it is. A kunya names a man by a son, so three kunyas point at three sons and at three moments in a household's life. [[NEEDS CLAIM: which sons the kunyas Abu Ibrahim, Abu al-Hasan and Abu 'Ali refer to]]. A man addressed by different kunyas in different reports is a man whose reports come from different decades and different circles.

Watch the designation reports and you can see that happening on the page. Al-Mufaddal calls him Abu Ibrahim when he walks into the room as a boy. Mu'adh b. Kathir's report has the father indicating al-'Abd al-Salih, asleep. Each transmitter uses the name his own circle used, and al-Mufid keeps their usage rather than standardising the lot of them into a single label for the convenience of his readers.

That decision costs a compiler something real. A clean text would call the man one thing throughout and would read better for it, and no reader would have complained. Al-Mufid takes the rougher option. The roughness is itself evidence: it shows the seams between the reports he is stitching together, and the seams are what a reader checking his work needs to see before deciding whether to trust him.

Two of the five names are not kunyas at all. Al-'Abd al-Salih is a description of practice. Al-Kazim is a description of temperament, and it is the one that stuck hard enough to name a city. [[NEEDS CLAIM: when the name al-Kazim first appears in a source, and in which]]. A description that becomes a name is a small piece of social history moving in slow motion.

A name of that kind also makes a claim about conduct. Restraint under provocation is a virtue with a politics attached: it says the man did not rise, did not raise a following in arms, did not answer the state on the state's own terms, and that all of this was a choice rather than a weakness. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any source connects the name al-Kazim to a specific episode]]. A name can carry an argument for centuries without ever making it.

Hold the name against the file. A man summoned out of Medina inside the caliph's own pilgrimage caravan, held at Basra under a kinsman of the caliph, moved on to Baghdad under al-Sindi b. Shahik, and dead in that prison in 183. The name and the custody describe the same behaviour from two directions, one admiring and one administrative. Neither of them proves the other, and a slide that treats them as one proof is cheating.

Names travel by a different route from facts. A date needs a source, and a source can be checked and found wanting. A name needs only people willing to go on using it. The ones that survive are the ones a community found useful, which makes the surviving name a piece of evidence about the community rather than about the man. [[NEEDS CLAIM: which of the five names dominates in al-Kafi's chains]].

One more name in the file belongs to the other side, and al-Mufid does not list it on page 407. The group who refused the death called him al-Muntazar, the awaited one, and they were calling him that while he was alive. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the earliest attestation of al-Muntazar applied to Musa b. Ja'far]]. A sixth name, held by the party that lost the argument and kept using it anyway.

So a panel of names is not decoration. Each of these five words records somebody's habit of speech, and the sixth records a doctrine that split a community. Al-Mufid hands you the five without comment on page 407. He hands you the sixth twenty pages later, in the middle of the account of the viewing on the bridge, where it explains why a jailer needed a crowd to look at a dead man's face.
The name that survived means the restrained one, and the men who chose it were describing a man the state had kept in a cell for the last four years of his life.

post.running_head: a list of obligations written as a list
post.caption:
The Risalat al-Huquq works downward: God, then the self, then the tongue,
the hearing, the sight, the hand, the leg, the stomach. Each one gets a
right against you. The document is built like an inventory, and the
inventory is the argument.

slides.body: the tongue
What kind of document lists your own tongue among the parties with a claim on you?

The Risalat al-Huquq opens with God and then turns to the body. The text says that God has given your tongue a right against you, your hearing a right, your sight a right, your hand, your leg, your stomach. Each organ is a creditor. The form is an inventory of debts, and a reader working down it meets the same construction eight times before the subject changes at all.

Repetition of that kind does work on a listener. The Arabic runs wa-amma haqq, and then, and then, and then. A man reciting it aloud sets a rhythm his audience can follow without a text in front of them. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether the Risalat al-Huquq was transmitted as a written letter or as an oral recitation]]. The shape of the sentence tells you something about the room it was made for.

Take the entry for the tongue on its own. The right of the tongue, the text says, is that you hold it above obscenity, accustom it to good, refrain from meddling in what gains nothing, express kindness to people, and speak well of them. Five clauses in one sentence. Two of them forbid something and three install a habit, and a habit takes years to install where a prohibition takes a decision. The proportion tells you which of the two the writer thought was the hard part.

Set that beside the entry for the self, which arrives one line earlier. The right of your self against you, the text says, is that you employ it in obeying God, and then deliver to the tongue its right, to the hearing its right, to the sight its right, and on down the body. The self is not one item among eight. It is the item that owes all the others, and the sentence makes that point by its grammar rather than by asserting it.

That ordering is the closest thing to a theory the document offers. It does not argue for a hierarchy. It does not defend one against a rival. It builds one out of the sequence in which the obligations arrive and leaves the reader to notice what has been built. A text that persuades by arrangement rather than by argument is a text expecting to be memorised, recited, and carried around in somebody's head where footnotes cannot follow it.

The manuscript history decides how much weight any of this carries. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the earliest source that transmits the Risalat al-Huquq, and its date]]. The Ansariyan edition on this shelf prints an English translation beside the Arabic with no critical apparatus at all. A reader checking a phrase has the translator's word, the Arabic facing it, and nothing in between: no variants, no manuscript sigla, no note explaining what the editor did where his copies disagreed.

That limit applies to almost everything in this corpus, and it is worth stating once in plain terms. A page number in a devotional edition tells you where a sentence sits in that printing. It tells you nothing about which manuscripts the editor used, how old they were, or what he did when they disagreed with each other. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether a critical edition of the Risalat al-Huquq exists]]. A citation is a location, and a location is not a guarantee.

What survives the limit is the structure, because structure is the part of a text that copying preserves best. Individual words drift between manuscripts. Whole clauses drop out and come back. The order of eight organs, each introduced by the same formula, does not drift, and two copies that disagreed about that order would be different documents rather than variant readings of one. Shape is the most durable evidence a text of this kind carries.

Compare that to how the same tradition handles a chronicle. Al-Kulayni's chains name the men who carried a report, so a reader can weigh it by them. The Risalat al-Huquq has no chain inside it at all: it is a text attributed to one man, standing on its own shape. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what chain al-Saduq or al-Harrani gives for the Risala]].
A document that assigns your own hearing a claim against you has stopped teaching ethics and started teaching accounting, and every line of it is built on that difference.
