post.running_head: a prisoner's letter about the mind
post.caption:
The longest thing attributed to Musa b. Ja'far is not about the caliphate.
It is a commandment addressed to Hisham b. al-Hakam about the mind, and
al-Harrani prints it at length in Tuhaf al-'Uqul.

Eighteen slides on what a man in custody chose to spend his words on.

slides.body: the commandment to hisham
What does a man under house arrest write about when he is free to write about anything?

Al-Harrani opens the section of maxims attributed to Musa b. Ja'far with a letter rather than a saying. It is addressed to Hisham b. al-Hakam and its subject is the mind. Not the succession, not the caliphs, not the men holding him. The compiler had a choice about what to lead with, and he led with a piece of argument about how a person reasons.

The opening move is a citation. God gives good news to those who listen to words and follow the best of them, and the letter quotes it before it says anything of its own. Starting on somebody else's authority is a choice about how to be read. The writer is placing his argument inside a text his correspondent already accepts.

Hisham b. al-Hakam is the reason the letter has the shape it has. [[NEEDS CLAIM: who Hisham b. al-Hakam was and what he was known for arguing]]. A letter about the mind addressed to a man known for disputation is not a devotional exercise written for a household. It is a contribution to an argument that already had participants, positions, opponents and a technical vocabulary, and the letter assumes all of that without stopping to explain any of it to a stranger.

The letter's claim is that God submitted his arguments to people through minds, and led them to his godhead through the same instrument. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the full wording of that passage in the Ansariyan translation, Tuhaf p. 124]]. Set out in flat terms, that is a position about where authority sits. Reason in it is no rival to revelation. Reason is the channel revelation arrives through, which makes an attack on reasoning an attack on the delivery of the message.

Positions like that had opponents in the same decades, and the letter reads one way against one opponent and another way against a different one. [[NEEDS CLAIM: which schools disputed the role of reason in the second century AH, and the source]]. This shelf holds the letter and not the argument it belonged to. That is the standard problem with a book of maxims: it keeps the answers and throws away the questions they were answers to.

Al-Harrani's own notes are the most useful thing on the page. He records that some of these sayings appear in different wording in al-Kafi, others in al-Khisal, and he prints the rival readings beside his own. That is unusual. A compiler who shows you a competing version of his own text is telling you where the text is soft, and inviting the comparison a modern reader would have to make anyway.

One of his notes shows the size of the problem. Where his copy has a man who corrects his evildoing by repentance, he records that al-Kafi has a man who corrects his guilt by repentance. One noun. That noun is the whole distance between an act and a state, between what a man did and what a man is, and a reader building anything on either word ought to know that the other one is sitting in a second manuscript a shelf away.

Another note reports a saying about the Divine Throne quivering for those who answer a question with the words God is the most knowledgeable. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the al-Kafi reference for that variant, from al-Harrani's note]]. Both versions praise the same refusal. Only one of them attaches a cosmic response to it, and that difference is worth a slide of its own.

Variants of that size accumulate into a real question about the genre. A book of maxims is assembled out of circulating material, and material circulates by being repeated from memory. Repetition edits. Nouns soften, clauses drop, a striking image attaches itself to a more famous name. The wonder is not that al-Harrani's copy differs from al-Kulayni's. It is that a compiler in that position bothered to write both readings down where a reader could see them.

Now put the letter back beside the biography. Al-Mufid's chapter on the same man is a case file: dates, custodians, a public viewing, a burial, a list of thirty-seven children with their mothers marked. Al-Harrani's chapter is a body of argument with no dates in it anywhere. Two compilers, one subject, almost no overlap in what either thought worth keeping, and both of them working inside the same tradition within a century of each other.

That divergence is no contradiction and should not be reported as one. A hadith collection and a biographical notice answer different questions, and the community that produced both saw no tension in doing so. A reader who wants the man rather than the office has to hold the two books open at once and accept that neither was written to satisfy the curiosity of somebody reading a thousand years later.

The custody hangs over the letter without appearing in it. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether Tuhaf al-'Uqul dates the commandment to Hisham, or places it in the custody]]. If the letter belongs to the years of detention, the choice of subject is remarkable. If it belongs to the years before, it is another document, and the sources on this shelf do not say which.

Dating a saying is harder than dating a death, which is why so few of these collections attempt it. A chronicle attaches an event to a year because the year is its organising principle and the entry has nowhere else to go. A maxim collection attaches a saying to a speaker. The speaker supplies a range of forty years, and forty years covers a man's youth, his succession, his arrests and the prison, which are four different situations to write from.

For this account the consequence is a rule about pillars, and it is worth stating as a rule rather than as a preference. A saying can carry a fact_panel, or a collision post about ideas, because both of those run on argument. A saying cannot carry a date_pair, a calendar or a number card, because all three of those need a date, and a saying does not have one to give.

A second rule sits next to the first one. Where a maxim collection and a chronicle disagree about a fact, the chronicle wins on chronology and the collection wins on wording, because each of them is closer to the thing it was built to preserve. Neither wins outright. A slide that hides the split and reports one of them as settled has stopped doing history and started doing publicity for a tradition.

Walking backwards is the whole method this account runs on. Find the sentence in the edition on the shelf. Note the printed page. Then ask which earlier book the editor took it from, whether that book survives, and whether anyone has collated the two. Most claims fail somewhere in that walk, and the second step is where. The few that survive all of it are the ones worth building a carousel around.

The commandment to Hisham survives the first two steps. It is printed, the page is fixed, the compiler names his variants, and the variants point at two other collections that also survive. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether al-Kafi carries the commandment to Hisham in full or in part]]. That is a stronger position than most of what a carousel about this man could stand on.
The state took his years, his household and at the end his life, and the text his own tradition chose to keep at greatest length is a letter arguing that a person should think.

Huyayy offering to share whatever happened. Fishbein's translation, page
15.

slides.body: the promise huyayy gave
What did one man have to promise another to make him break a treaty?

Al-Tabari keeps the conversation itself. Huyayy b. Akhtab tells Ka'b b. Asad that Quraysh and Ghatafan are encamped at Dhanab Naqama beside Uhud with their leaders and their chiefs, and that they have made a treaty and covenant with him not to withdraw until they root out Muhammad and everyone with him. That is the pitch in one sentence: overwhelming force, already committed, already in position, and a named place a listener could ride out and look at before morning.

Ka'b does not believe a word of it. He tells Huyayy that he has brought him everlasting humiliation, and calls the promised army a cloud that has already shed its water, a cloud that thunders and lightens and has nothing left in it. A man who refuses a military alliance in a weather metaphor is a man who has watched coalitions gather before, and watched them go home again with nothing done and his own position worse for having joined.

Then comes the sentence that makes the passage worth a carousel. Leave me to continue with Muhammad as I am now, Ka'b says, for I have seen nothing from Muhammad except truth and faithfulness. That is a Jewish chief of Medina, quoted inside a Muslim chronicle, giving his reason for keeping a treaty. The chronicle did not have to keep it.

Chroniclers keep what their material gives them and what their argument can carry, and this line makes the break that follows worse rather than better. It establishes on the record that Ka'b knew the treaty was working, that he said so out loud, and that he broke it anyway. A compiler protecting a reputation would have cut it. [[NEEDS CLAIM: which of al-Tabari's named authorities this report comes through, in Fishbein's volume VIII]].

Huyayy keeps wheedling. That is the translator's word, and Fishbein footnotes it. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the Arabic verb behind Fishbein's wheedling, and his note on it]]. A translator's choice at a hinge like this decides how a reader hears the whole exchange: wheedling makes Huyayy small and Ka'b weak, where a colder verb would leave two men negotiating. An English page number is a weaker citation than an Arabic one for this reason.

What moves Ka'b in the end is not the argument. It is a bond. Huyayy gives a promise and an oath by God that if Quraysh and Ghatafan retreat without having killed Muhammad, he will enter the fortress with Ka'b, so that whatever happens to Ka'b happens to him. He is not offering better odds or a larger army. He is offering to stand inside the consequences of his own advice.

Read as politics, that is a man with nothing left to trade putting his own body on the table. Read as narrative, it is the chronicle stating why the treaty broke: one man accepting personal risk, with no zeal and no doctrine in it, in front of another man who had already called his bluff. Ka'b then broke his treaty, the chronicle says, and renounced the bond that had existed between him and the Prophet.

The clause about renouncing a bond is doing legal work in that sentence. A treaty here is a document with conditions and a formal way out, and the chronicle marks that Ka'b used the exit rather than acting without one. That detail survives because somebody in the chain thought the procedure mattered. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the treaty between the Prophet and the Banu Qurayza is reported to have contained]].

That question matters because the rest of the episode turns on it, and this shelf holds the volume that narrates it. What the shelf does not hold is a second independent chronicle of the same week. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether Ibn Ishaq via Guillaume carries the same conversation, and at what page]]. Guillaume is on the shelf; the check is an afternoon's work.

Doing that check is how a carousel earns the right to quote a conversation from the year 5. Two chronicles preserving the same exchange, with different chains of transmission behind them, is evidence that something like it was being told early. One chronicle preserving it, quoted twice in two different posts, is one chronicle wearing a second coat, and a reader has no way to tell the difference from the slide.

The SUNY volume has to be registered before any of this can be verified. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the edition statement, translator's name and ISBN of the volume on this shelf]]. The manifest records Fishbein as the translator, leaves the edition as TODO, and the database refuses to verify a claim against a TODO edition. Nothing in this carousel can go past draft until somebody copies four lines off a title page.

Care is owed here for a second reason beyond the citation mechanics. This is a Jewish clan in a Muslim chronicle, on the way to an outcome that later readers argue about at length. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what happened to the Banu Qurayza after the siege, according to the volume on this shelf]]. Reporting what a page says, and naming the page, is the account's whole method. It holds hardest where the subject is hardest.

What the page says here is narrow, and worth stating as it stands. Two men talked in a fortress. One had a coalition to sell and no credibility left. The other had a working treaty, an accurate read of the odds, and no appetite for war. The sale went through on a personal guarantee. The chronicle names both men, names the camp, and keeps the refusal that came before the agreement.
Ka'b broke a treaty he had just described as working, and the price was one man's promise to share the outcome.

post.running_head: what a chronicler does with a story he doubts
post.caption:
Ibn Ishaq reports that 'A'isha heard Isaf and Na'ila were a man and a
woman turned to stone for what they did in the Ka'ba. Then he writes: but
God alone knows if this is the truth.

Guillaume, page 38. A source marking its own uncertainty is the most
useful thing on a page.

slides.body: isaf and naila
How does a chronicler tell you he does not believe the story he has just written down?

Ibn Ishaq gives the story with a chain attached. It runs through 'Amra to 'A'isha, and what 'A'isha said is that they always heard Isaf and Na'ila were a man and a woman of Jurham who copulated in the Ka'ba, and that God turned them into two stones. Then Ibn Ishaq adds six words of his own: but God alone knows if this is the truth. He does not cut the story and he does not endorse it.

That formula is a working tool rather than a piety. It marks a report as carried rather than confirmed, and it does the marking in public, on the same line, where no later copyist can drop it without leaving a hole. A modern historian uses a footnote for that job. Ibn Ishaq had no footnotes, so the qualification travels inside the sentence, and it has travelled with the sentence for thirteen hundred years and through every hand that copied it.

Watch what it lets him do. The origin story for two named stones in the sanctuary is material his readers already knew, and leaving it out would have looked like concealment. Printing it flat would have committed him to it. The formula gives him a third option: the story is in the record, the reader knows where it came from, and the compiler's own weight stays off it.

Compare that with how the same page handles ordinary practice. Every household had an idol in the house, Ibn Ishaq writes, and a man about to set out on a journey would rub himself against it before riding off, and rub himself against it again when he came back before going in to his family. No chain, no qualification, no doubt marker. He is describing a custom he expects nobody to dispute.

The difference between those two passages is the whole method in one page. A claim about a miracle in the deep past gets a chain and a disclaimer. A claim about what people did before a journey gets neither, because everyone reading in the second century still had grandparents who remembered doing it. Confidence tracks how close the evidence sits to the writer.

[[NEEDS CLAIM: whether Guillaume notes a variant or an alternative account of Isaf and Na'ila]]. Guillaume's apparatus matters here because the translation on this shelf is OCR of a print copy, and the page numbers in the margin are Ibn Hisham's Arabic pagination rather than the English one. A citation to page 38 of an English translation is a citation to a particular printing.

The tawaghit paragraph on the same page widens the picture. Alongside the Ka'ba the Arabs had temples they venerated the way they venerated the Ka'ba, with guardians and overseers, and they circumambulated them and sacrificed at them. That is a description of a system with staff, revenue and procedure, and it is set down in three lines with no argument attached.

Staff and revenue are the part a political historian reaches for. A sanctuary with overseers is an institution, and an institution has an interest in the arrangements that fund it. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what Ibn Ishaq says about who held the guardianship of the Ka'ba, and where]]. The sira gives the pieces and declines to assemble them, which is what leaves later readers so much room.

One line on the page shows the pressure the account was written under. When God sent Muhammad with the message of monotheism, Ibn Ishaq writes, Quraysh said: would he make the gods into one God, that is a strange proceeding. The objection is quoted in the objectors' own voice, without a rebuttal following it. A compiler confident of his case can afford to let the other side speak.

A carousel can take one of two things from this page. Either the content, which is the furniture of pre-Islamic Mecca, or the method, which is a writer sorting his material by how far he will stand behind it. The second is the better post, because it hands a reader a tool they can use on the next page and on this account.

Using that tool here means saying which of these claims this account would stand behind. The household idols, yes: reported flat, without a chain and without a hedge, by a writer close enough to living memory that his readers could have corrected him. The two stones, no: reported with a chain and a disclaimer by the writer himself. This account has no business being more certain than Ibn Ishaq was about his own material.

[[NEEDS CLAIM: whether al-Tabari's Arabic carries the Isaf and Na'ila report, and with what qualification]]. That check would show whether the disclaimer travelled with the story or was attached once and dropped afterwards. A story that gains certainty as it moves between books is a story to trust less at each stop, not more, and the six words Ibn Ishaq added are the control that makes the comparison possible.
The most valuable six words on that page are the ones where the writer steps back from his own sentence, and every compiler after him kept them.

post.running_head: one flag, priced twice, in two currencies
post.caption:
Subhani puts a price on the Sasanian battle standard: 1,200,000 dirhams,
or 30,000 pounds. The second figure is a translator converting for a
reader in the twentieth century, and the two numbers are not the same kind
of fact.

slides.body: twelve hundred thousand dirhams
When a modern book prices an object from the sixth century in two currencies at once, which of the two numbers is the evidence, and which one is the author talking to you?

Subhani is setting the scene before Islam and reaches for the Sasanian court. The flag called Dirafsh-i Kavyani went up in the battlefield or stood at the top of the palace on ceremonial days. It was studded with gems, he writes, and according to a writer the cost has been estimated at 1,200,000 dirhams, or 30,000 pounds. Two figures, one sentence, and a footnote hanging off the end of it.

Separate the two numbers before doing anything else with them. The 1,200,000 dirhams is a figure Subhani attributes to somebody: according to a writer, he says, and the note points at the source. [[NEEDS CLAIM: which writer Subhani's footnote 2 on page 43 names]]. The 30,000 pounds is nobody's medieval figure. It is a conversion, done for a reader who thinks in pounds.

Conversions rot. A sum in pounds carries an exchange rate and a year inside it, and the moment either of those moves the number stops meaning what it meant on the day it was set in type. A reader quoting 30,000 pounds today is quoting a translator's arithmetic from the decade the book went to press, at a silver price nobody wrote down. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the year this translation of The Message was printed]]. The pound has moved since. So has the silver.

The dirham figure carries its own problem, and it is the older one. A dirham is a weight of silver before it is a coin, and the weight moved between periods and between mints. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the standard weight of a dirham in the Sasanian period and in the first century AH]]. Without that figure, 1,200,000 dirhams is a large number rather than a quantity of metal, and a large number is a feeling somebody wants you to have.

Feeling is what the figure was made to produce. It sits in a paragraph about the fondness of the Sasanian court for luxury, whose pomp dazzled the eyes. That is the argument the number is serving. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether Subhani's source gives the estimate as a contemporary valuation or as a later reckoning]]. An estimate made three centuries after the object was melted down is a different object.

A number card in this account states its arithmetic and the two dates it spans. Here the arithmetic is a division nobody can perform. Take 1,200,000 dirhams, divide by an unknown weight, in an unknown year, against an unrecorded silver price, then convert at an unstated rate to reach 30,000 pounds. Four unknowns and one product. That is a rhetorical figure wearing the clothes of a measurement, and the clothes are the whole effect.

So the honest version of this card reports the sentence instead of the sum. Subhani, writing in the twentieth century, cites a writer who estimated the Sasanian standard at 1,200,000 dirhams, and his translator sets 30,000 pounds beside it. Every element of that is checkable against the page. None of it requires anyone to know what the flag was worth, which is fortunate, because nobody does.

That is a smaller claim and a much stronger one. It survives a reader who knows more about Sasanian metrology than the writer does, which is the test any figure on a slide has to pass before it goes out. The alternative is a caption announcing that the flag was worth thirty thousand pounds, which will be wrong in a way no reader can trace back to the decision that made it wrong.

The card needs two dates to stand at all, and the page supplies neither. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the years of the Sasanian reign Subhani is describing on page 43]]. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the year of the edition of The Message on this shelf, from its title page]]. One date places the object. The other places the estimate. Between them sits the gap the whole figure has to cross, and on the rough count that gap runs to 1,400 years of other people's arithmetic.

Until those two rows exist this stays a draft, and the machinery in the repository enforces that rather than trusting anybody's memory. The manifest carries no edition statement for SRC-SUB-001, so nothing citing it can be verified. The linter counts the placeholders above and refuses the render. Two independent locks, and the card cannot become a picture by accident or by somebody being in a hurry on a Sunday night.
A price in two currencies is one estimate and one act of translation, and the slide that repeats both without saying which is which has invented a fact out of a footnote.

post.running_head: two days between an agreement and a night attack
post.caption:
The commentary in this Nahj al-Balagha edition says the arriving army
agreed that 'Uthman b. Hunayf would stay at his post until Ali reached
Basra. Two days later they attacked him at night and killed forty people.

An agreement with a two-day life is a fact about the agreement.

slides.body: the governor at basra
How long did the agreement at Basra hold before somebody broke it?

The commentary attached to this edition gives a number that does the whole argument. When the army reached Basra, the governor 'Uthman b. Hunayf came out to stop them, and terms were reached: the existing administration would continue until Ali arrived. Two days later they made a night attack on him and killed forty people. Not a season. Not a month. Two days, and the settlement was over.

A truce that dies in two days tells you what it was for. Nobody arriving with an army needs forty-eight hours to change their mind about a political arrangement they have just accepted. They need forty-eight hours to get inside a city, find the guard posts, count the men the governor can call on before dawn, and learn which gate stays open. The agreement bought reconnaissance, and it was paid for in words.

That is a reading rather than a report, and the difference has to stay visible on the slide. What the page states is a sequence: agreement, two days, a night attack, forty dead. What a reader adds is a motive. Motives are cheap. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any early source gives a reason for the two-day delay at Basra]]. Until that row exists, the sequence is the claim and everything built on top of it is a suggestion wearing a confident tone.

The commentary is also a source with a position, and this account says so rather than hiding it. It is printed inside a Shia edition of Nahj al-Balagha, arranged to explain the setting of a letter by Ali. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the name of the commentator and translator of this edition, from the title page]]. The manifest lists both as TODO.

Position does not settle whether a report is true, and it does decide which questions get asked. A commentary written to introduce Ali's letter will count the dead at Basra and will not spend a paragraph on what the other side thought it had agreed to. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what al-Tabari's volumes on the year 36 say about the Basra agreement]]. Those volumes are not on this shelf.

The people in the paragraph before it are named, which helps a reader test any of it. On reaching Mecca, the commentary says, 'A'isha began rousing people to avenge 'Uthman's blood by circulating stories of his having been victimised. The first to respond was 'Abdullah b. 'Amir al-Hadrami, who had been governor of Mecca in 'Uthman's own reign. With him came Marwan b. al-Hakam and Sa'id b. al-'As.

Read that list as a roster rather than as a narrative. Al-Hadrami, a former governor. Marwan b. al-Hakam and Sa'id b. al-'As, both Umayyads. Ya'la b. Munabbih, former governor of Yemen. 'Abdullah b. 'Amir b. Kurayz, former governor of Basra. Four of the first movers had held office under the killed caliph, and two of them had held the two cities the war was about to be fought in.

Men who have run a province know its treasury, its garrison and its grain stores. A coalition of former governors arrives with logistics already inside it. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the sources say about the funds and troops these men brought to Basra]]. One figure would turn a list of names into an account of how the campaign was paid for, and paying for a campaign is the part of a civil war that nobody writes a sermon about.

The same paragraph reports that Talha and al-Zubayr reached Mecca from Medina. Both had stood at the centre of the succession weeks earlier. Their arrival changes the character of the gathering from a protest about a killing into a claim on the office, and the commentary records the journey without remarking on the change. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the dates of Talha and al-Zubayr's departure from Medina]]. A month either way rewrites the sequence.

Now come back to the forty dead. The commentary calls them innocent persons, and that adjective is the commentator's, not the record's. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any source names the men killed in the night attack at Basra, or their standing]]. A number with an adjective attached is doing two jobs, and a slide should carry the number and leave the adjective to the reader.

This account will print forty, attributed to the commentary, and will leave innocent off the slide. The men may well have been bystanders. The reason for the omission is procedural: the count and the characterisation come from the same page, and one of the two can be checked against another book while the other cannot. Print what a stranger could go and verify, and leave the adjective to whoever verifies it.

Checking is the part this shelf cannot do yet. [[NEEDS CLAIM: which SUNY volume covers the year 36 and the events at Basra]]. Volume VIII stops at the Medina years, volume XL is an index with no narrative in it, and the Arabic OpenITI text carries the whole chronicle but needs somebody who reads Arabic to work the relevant year. Three volumes on the shelf, and none of them answers the question without help.

The Arabic is the shortest route and it is sitting in the corpus already. A search of SRC-TAB-AR for the year 36 would produce the annalistic entry in a few minutes. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the Arabic al-Tabari enters under the year 36 about 'Uthman b. Hunayf]]. That is one afternoon between this draft and a carousel that stands on two independent sources.
A governor kept his post for two days on the strength of an agreement, and the men who signed it came for him in the dark.

post.running_head: what a modern book denies, and who it is answering
post.caption:
Al-Qarashi's book on the twelfth Imam spends a paragraph denying something
its own community is accused of holding: that the reappearance comes from
the cellar at Samarra. A denial tells you what the accusation was.

slides.body: not from the cellar
Why would a book spend a paragraph denying a belief nobody in it holds?

Al-Qarashi's volume on the twelfth Imam stops mid-argument to deny a specific claim. Shias have announced, and go on announcing, that the reappearance of the Master of the Age will not be from the cellar of Samarra. The place, he writes, is Mecca. Nothing in the paragraph explains who said otherwise, and the denial is written as though every reader already knows.

Every reader in his intended audience did know. The cellar at Samarra is a fixture of polemic against Twelver Shi'ism, repeated in argument for centuries, and it turns a doctrine about occultation into an image of people waiting at a hole in the ground. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the earliest polemical text that attributes the cellar belief to the Shia, and its date]].

A denial is evidence about the accusation rather than about the doctrine. It tells a historian that the charge was live enough, and irritating enough, that a twentieth-century author writing a devotional life would break his own narrative to answer it. That is the useful fact on the page, and it can be reported without anyone taking a position on occultation itself.

This account does not adjudicate that question and will not. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the earliest Imami sources say about the place of the reappearance]]. A stranger reading this carousel owes the tradition nothing and has no reason to accept a claim about the end of history from a picture on a phone. A slide that asks them to hold a belief before the sentence makes sense has failed the register rule this whole account is written under.

What can be described is the argumentative move. Al-Qarashi compares the disappearance to the Prophet leaving Mecca for Yathrib while his house stood surrounded, with 'Ali sleeping in his bed. The comparison converts a metaphysical claim into a tactical one. A man in danger left, having arranged a substitute, and the watchers outside the door failed to notice until the morning. Stated that way, the story needs no metaphysics at all.

That is a rhetorical strategy with a long history and it is worth naming as one. Anchor the contested event to an uncontested event in the same tradition, and the reader's acceptance of the second does part of the work for the first. Whether the analogy holds is a question for a theologian. That it is being used is a question of reading.

Notice what the paragraph does not do. It cites nothing. No chain, no earlier author, no page number, no volume. The claim about what Shias have announced arrives as common knowledge, inside a book that carries footnotes elsewhere and uses them with some care. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether al-Qarashi cites a source for the cellar denial anywhere in the volume]]. The absence is the interesting part of the page.

An uncited paragraph in a cited book marks the line between what an author argues and what he assumes. Assumptions get no footnotes because the author cannot imagine anybody needing one. For a reader standing outside the tradition, those are the passages worth slowing down on: they show where the book expects agreement rather than persuasion, and agreement is where a community keeps its actual furniture.

The translation adds a layer. The English on this shelf renders phrases like Master of the Age and the gate of the city of his knowledge, and each of those is a decision. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the translator of the Ansariyan edition of al-Qarashi's Life of Imam al-Mahdi, from the title page]]. The manifest lists it as TODO, so nothing citing this book can be verified yet.

Registering it matters more here than for a chronicle. A twentieth-century devotional work is a source for twentieth-century belief and argument, which is a real historical subject with dates of its own. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the year of publication of this volume]]. Without that year the book floats loose in time. A reader cannot tell which decade's polemics it answers, or whose accusation it judged worth a paragraph of denial.

That is the honest frame for a carousel about this page: a modern author, writing at a datable moment, answering a charge older than he is, in a book with no footnote at that point. Every element of that is checkable from the title page and the paragraph itself, and none of it requires a reader to hold any belief about the twelfth Imam.
The sentence a book writes without a footnote is the sentence it never expected to have to defend, and those are the ones that tell you who it thinks is listening.

post.running_head: a sanctuary that was one of several
post.caption:
Ibn Ishaq writes that alongside the Ka'ba the Arabs had tawaghit: temples
they venerated the same way, with guardians and overseers, which they
circled and sacrificed at.

A map post with no coordinates on it, because the source gives none.

slides.body: the other temples
How many sanctuaries were there, and does any source on this shelf say where they stood?

Ibn Ishaq puts the whole system in three lines. Alongside the Ka'ba the Arabs had adopted tawaghit, which were temples they venerated the way they venerated the Ka'ba. Those temples had their guardians and overseers. People made offerings to them, circled them, and sacrificed at them. The verbs are the same verbs used of the Ka'ba, which is the point of the sentence and the reason it is worth a carousel. Nobody circles a shrine they think is minor.

Sameness of ritual implies a network rather than a hierarchy. A pilgrim who circles one shrine and sacrifices at another is moving through a landscape with several fixed points in it, and each point has staff who eat from the offerings. [[NEEDS CLAIM: how many tawaghit Ibn Ishaq names, and where the sira places them]]. Without those names this map has one certain location on it and an unknown number of blanks.

A map post with blanks is still a map post, provided the blanks are drawn as blanks. The failure mode of this format is a clean line between two dots on a modern basemap, which tells a reader that somebody knows the route. Nobody on this shelf knows the route between the Meccan sanctuary and any of the others, because the source names neither the roads nor most of the shrines.

What the source does supply is scale at the domestic end. Every household had an idol in the house, Ibn Ishaq writes, and a man setting out on a journey rubbed himself against it before riding, and rubbed himself against it again on returning before going in to his family. That gives a third tier: household, local temple, and the sanctuary at Mecca.

Three tiers is a structure a reader can hold, and it changes what the later argument is about. A message of one God arriving in that landscape is not only correcting a doctrine. It is removing a fixture from every house, a revenue stream from every temple staff, and the ritual that opened and closed every journey. Furniture is harder to argue with than doctrine, and it is what the objection reaches for.

Ibn Ishaq puts the objection in Quraysh's own words a line later. Would he make the gods into one God, they say, that is a strange proceeding. Read beside the household idols, that reads less like theology and more like a man being told the furniture is going. The compiler leaves the two sentences next to each other and adds nothing.

For a map post the useful question is where the guardians came from. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether the sira names the clans holding the guardianship of any sanctuary besides the Ka'ba]]. Guardianship is heritable, local and lucrative, so the answer would locate several of these temples by naming the families who ran them, which is how ancient geography gets recovered. Guardianship is the thread that leads back to the temples named at the top of this essay.

The Ka'ba itself is the one fixed point, and even its furniture gets named. Isaf and Na'ila are two stones with an origin story attached, and Abu Talib's verse in the same passage places them where the pilgrims make their camels kneel and the waters flow. That is a topographic detail inside a poem, and poems preserve topography better than prose does.

Where the pilgrims make their camels kneel is a real instruction. It tells you the stones stood at the point where a caravan stopped, which is the busiest and most valuable ground in any sanctuary. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what Guillaume's notes say about the location of Isaf and Na'ila]]. A note there would turn a line of verse into a position on a plan.

Yaqut would settle a good deal of this, and Yaqut is the gap in this corpus. The Wustenfeld edition downloaded from archive.org came back as unreadable OCR, so the standard geographical dictionary of the Arabic tradition sits on the shelf in a form nothing can search. [[NEEDS CLAIM: a usable text of Mu'jam al-buldan]]. The dictionary that would fill this map is a nineteenth century book, and the copy this pipeline fetched is unreadable.

That single missing book is why this account has no distances in it. Not one carousel here states how far Medina lies from Mecca, or Basra from Baghdad, and every attempt to write such a sentence has produced a placeholder instead. A pipeline that renders placeholders as failures makes the shape of a missing source visible. That single missing dictionary is the reason every distance in this account is bracketed.

Visible is better than filled. A map slide with a blank on it invites a reader to ask what would fill it, and the answer here is one nineteenth century edition, in Arabic, with a text layer somebody can search. That is a specific, purchasable, solvable problem rather than a vague complaint about sources. A blank drawn as a blank is still a map, and it names the book that would finish it.

The sanctuary at Mecca stands on this map because a poem happened to name the ground it sat on, and every other temple in the passage has no location at all. The temples in that sentence had staff, revenue and a location, and only the staff survive in the record.

post.running_head: a chronicle that files a siege under a year
post.cover_title: the events of the year five
post.caption:
Fishbein's volume VIII prints a running head across its pages: The Events
of the Year 5. Everything inside that heading happened, as far as the
chronicle is concerned, in one unit of time.

What a chronicle can date, and what it cannot, decides what a carousel
can claim.

slides.body: the events of the year five
What can a reader date to a day, and what can a reader only date to a year?

Open Fishbein's volume at the siege and the running head answers before the text does. The Events of the Year 5. Everything under that heading sits in one bin. A conversation in a fortress, a coalition camped beside Uhud, a treaty broken, an outcome: the chronicle gives all of it a single temporal address, and the address is a year rather than a month or a morning.

Annalistic form is a decision about storage, and storage decides retrieval. A compiler working year by year can tell you which events belong to the same twelve months, which is useful, and cannot tell you the order of two events inside those months unless he says so. Most of the time he does not say so, because his own sources did not. Order inside the bin is the reader's problem.

That limitation reaches the slide itself. A carousel can state that the conversation between Huyayy b. Akhtab and Ka'b b. Asad falls in the year 5 on al-Tabari's arrangement. It cannot state the month without a source saying so. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether volume VIII gives a month for the siege or for the Qurayza episode]]. The year heading is the finest resolution the chronicle offers.

Compare the other end of this account's material. Al-Kulayni dates the summons of Musa b. Ja'far out of Medina to the twentieth of Shawwal in 179, a day inside a month inside a year, and that precision is what makes a date_pair post possible at all. One tradition preserved an administrative note. The other preserved a year heading. Al-Kulayni had a note from a registry; al-Tabari had a year and a list.

Neither is more honest than the other. They are answering different questions with different material, and a reader who treats a year heading as vagueness has misread the genre. The heading is a claim: these things belong together in time. Given how much of the record for that decade is unanchored, that is a substantial claim rather than a hedge.

The claim can be tested, which is the useful part. If a second chronicle files the same events under the year 5, the two agree on grouping. If one files them under 4 or 6, the disagreement is visible at once and can be reported on a slide. [[NEEDS CLAIM: which year Ibn Ishaq via Guillaume assigns to the siege and to the Qurayza episode]].

Both books sit on this shelf, so that check costs one afternoon and produces a real result either way. Agreement gives a carousel two independent witnesses to a grouping. Disagreement gives a better carousel: two chronicles, two years, and a reader watching a tradition sort itself out in front of them. Two books, one shelf, one afternoon, and a result either way.

The year itself needs converting before a modern reader can place it, and conversion is its own trap. A hijri year overlaps two Gregorian years, so a single AH date maps to a range and not to a point. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the Gregorian span of AH 5, and the source used for the conversion]]. A year that maps to a range cannot be printed as a point without inventing the difference. Six hundred years earlier, the caution grows.

This repository has a tool that does that conversion and refuses to be trusted about it. It reports a tabular Hijri date, states that a sighted calendar can differ by a day, and near a boundary tells the operator to check a published calendar instead. The same caution applies to a year six hundred years earlier, with more force rather than less.

Named places are the other anchor a date_pair post can lean on. Dhanab Naqama beside Uhud is a specific camp beside a specific hill, and Uhud is a landmark that has not moved. A reader can stand there. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what Fishbein's note says about the location of Dhanab Naqama]]. Uhud has not moved, and a reader can stand on it.

Place and year together give a carousel its two coordinates, and the pair is stronger than either alone. The year 5, beside Uhud, in the fortress of a named clan, with two named men talking. Nothing in that sentence requires a month, and a reader who wants a month has learned something about the record rather than about the event. Fifteen is a printing, not a text.

The volume also has to be registered before any of this can be verified. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the edition statement and ISBN of the SUNY volume VIII on this shelf]]. The manifest names Michael Fishbein as translator and State University of New York Press as publisher, and leaves the edition as TODO, which blocks verification by design. Registration is four lines copied off a title page, and it blocks everything until somebody copies them.

Registration matters more for a translation than for an original. Page 15 of Fishbein is not page 15 of anything else, and a claim citing it names a printing rather than a text. The Arabic pagination in the margin is the durable address. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the de Goeje page numbers printed in the margins of volume VIII at this passage]].

Those marginal numbers are the reason the OpenITI Arabic text matters even to a reader who works in English. If a slide cites de Goeje's page alongside Fishbein's, any reader with either book can find the sentence. That is what a citation is for, and it costs nothing but the discipline of copying two numbers instead of one. Copy both numbers.

A date_pair post is not always two dates. Sometimes it is a date and the shape of a date: a year on one side, a day on the other, and an honest account of why the two sides of the pair are made of different material. That is a harder slide to write and a more useful one to read.
The chronicle knows which year the treaty broke in and does not know which morning, and a carousel that supplies the morning has stopped quoting it.

post.running_head: a chapter that exists to answer one objection
post.caption:
Ibn Babawayh opens 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida with a chapter whose title is a
question: why is 'Ali b. Musa called al-Rida. A compiler who opens with
that question is answering somebody.

slides.body: why they call him al-rida
Why would a book open by explaining a name its readers already use every day?

Ibn Babawayh gives his first chapter a question for a title: why is 'Ali b. Musa called al-Rida. Chapter one, before the biography, before the reports, before anything else. A compiler who spends his opening on a name is not filling space. He is answering an objection loud enough that his readers would have met it before they met his book.

The objection appears a few pages earlier in the same volume, phrased as opponents think. They say al-Ma'mun called him al-Rida, meaning acceptable or liked, and the name therefore records a caliph's approval rather than anything else. Put that way, the title becomes a piece of Abbasid patronage attached to a man the tradition venerates. The name arrives attached to a caliph's decision, and that is the whole objection. Chapter one, before anything else.

That is a sharp attack because it uses the tradition's own material. The caliph did raise 'Ali b. Musa up, and the elevation is not in dispute anywhere. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what al-Ma'mun's arrangement with 'Ali b. Musa consisted of, and the year]]. A name that arrives with an appointment looks like part of the appointment. Elevation is not in dispute; what the name records is. The name would then be a gift. Read that way, the title is an Abbasid label, and chapter one exists to take it back.

Ibn Babawayh answers with a chain rather than an argument, and the choice of instrument is the interesting part. The chapter opens on a list of transmitters: his father, then Muhammad b. Musa b. al-Mutawakkil, then Muhammad b. 'Ali b. Majiluwayh, then Ahmad b. 'Ali b. Ibrahim b. Hashim, and more after them. The reply to a claim about politics is a list of names.

That move only works on a reader who already accepts what a chain is for. A chain says: this report reached me through these men, weigh it by them. A reader outside the tradition has no way to weigh those men without a biographical dictionary, and the dictionaries are themselves works of the tradition. The argument is closed to a stranger without help.

Supplying that help is the job this account takes on, and the way to do it is not to assert that the chain is sound. [[NEEDS CLAIM: how the rijal literature grades the transmitters named in the first chain of 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida]]. State who they were, state who graded them and when, and let a reader see the machinery rather than the verdict. A stranger cannot weigh the men in that chain without a second library.

Ibn Babawayh also names himself in full on the page: Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. 'Ali b. Husayn b. Musa b. Babwaih al-Qumi, resident of Ray. That is a man from Qum living in Ray, writing about a grave in Tus, for a community spread across three provinces. The geography of the book is worth a carousel of its own. State the machinery, and let the reader reach the verdict.

The poem printed just before the chapter heading gives the same geography from the other side. It sends greetings to a master at Tus, carried by a visitor who got up early and walked like lightning. A devotional poem that names a destination is telling you people were going there. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the poet's name and date, from this edition]]. Qum, Ray and Tus are three provinces and one argument.

Visitors going to Tus in numbers is a political fact before it is a devotional one. A grave that draws travellers is a place where a community assembles, counts itself and is counted by other people. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the sources say about visits to the grave at Tus in the third century AH]]. People were walking to that grave, and somebody wrote a poem for them to carry. Somebody walked, and somebody wrote it down.

All of which sits behind a chapter that looks, from its title, like etymology. Why is he called al-Rida. The answer decides whether a name records a caliph's favour or something the community held first, and the compiler thought it important enough to spend his opening pages on it. Counting is what a state notices. A grave that draws travellers becomes a place where a community counts itself, and counting is what a state notices about a crowd.
A book that begins by defending a name is telling you the name was being used against it.

post.running_head: sixty days a year when the design changes and nobody is asked
post.caption:
From Muharram 1 to Safar 30 this account changes its own design: solid
covers, a night ground, bone ink, no ornament. Sixty days out of every
lunar year, decided by a calendar the pipeline is not allowed to guess at.

slides.body: muharram to safar
Who decides which sixty days a publication looks different, and what happens when the machine gets it wrong?

The window is fixed and needs nobody's confirmation. Muharram 1 to Safar 30, two lunar months, about fifty-nine days. Inside it every cover in this account goes solid, the ground drops to near black, the ink lifts to bone, and the ornament comes off. Outside it the covers carry duotoned images and the ground is paper. One boundary, two designs, no middle setting.

A design that changes on a date is a promise to a reader. It says the account knows what season it is, and that somebody is paying attention on a morning when a cheerful image would land wrong. Getting it right is unremarkable. Getting it wrong once undoes the promise for every reader who noticed, and the ones who noticed are the ones who cared.

So the question becomes mechanical. What decides the date, and what is the machine allowed to do with it? The answer in this repository is narrow on purpose: a tool converts a Gregorian date to a Hijri date by arithmetic, reports both, and stops. It never flips a token. It never writes to the database. It advises, and a person acts.

The arithmetic it uses is the tabular Islamic calendar, a fixed cycle that assigns each year a pattern of long and short months. It is exact, reproducible and independent of the sky. It is also not the calendar anybody keeps Muharram by, because that one is set by sighting the moon, and sighting depends on weather, latitude and a judgement.

The two can differ by a day, and now and then by two. That is small arithmetic and a large editorial problem, because the difference lands on the boundary where the design changes. A day early and the account is in mourning while everyone else is not. A day late and it publishes an ornamented cover on the first morning of Muharram. Weather decides it, and weather is local.

The tool therefore does something unusual for a piece of software: near a boundary it refuses to answer. It prints the tabular date, says a sighted calendar can differ, and tells the operator to check the published calendar before posting. A program that declines to decide is a program whose author knew which errors were expensive. The reference is published, dated and public, which is what makes it usable at all. Expensive errors deserve a program that stops.

Sistani's published calendar is the reference this account follows, and the wafat dates come from it. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the wafat dates as published in Sistani's calendar, month and day]]. The file holding them lists twelve entries and every one of them still says TODO, so the mourning check today covers the two month window and nothing else. An empty list that announces itself is safe.

The tool reports that gap every time it runs. Twelve wafat dates are still TODO, it says, so this answer covers Muharram and Safar only. An empty list that stays quiet would let a wafat date pass with the ordinary design on it, and nobody would find out until a reader wrote in. A wafat date that slips past with an ornamented cover on it is the one failure this design cannot apologise its way out of.

Filling those twelve entries is a religious determination and not a research task, which is why no part of this pipeline attempts it. A model guessing a wafat date from memory would be inventing a fact of the kind this whole system exists to prevent, and it would be inventing it about something people mark by fasting. Rajab sits outside the window and inside the list.

The same reasoning governs the death this account keeps returning to. Al-Mufid dates it to the sixth of Rajab in 183. Rajab is not Muharram and is not Safar, so that day falls outside the two month window and belongs on the wafat list instead. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether 6 Rajab appears on Sistani's published wafat list]]. Bookkeeping decides what a reader sees on the morning it matters.

Notice how much of a calendar post is bookkeeping rather than history. Which day, on whose authority, in which of two calendars, checked against which published list. None of that is interesting to read and all of it decides what a reader sees. The interesting part sits on top of it and cannot stand without it. A season is not an anniversary.

Here is the interesting part. A community that keeps sixty days of mourning every year is keeping a season, not an anniversary. Seasons change what a whole society does: markets, weddings, music, the colour people wear. An account that publishes into that season and ignores it is speaking over the top of its readers. A dark ground says the account noticed, and says nothing else.

The design response can go two ways and this one takes the quieter route. A dark ground and a bone ink is a change anyone notices at a glance in a feed. It carries no image, no ornament and no argument about how anybody should feel. The account keeps publishing evidence, and it does so on a different sheet of paper. Three reasons, one outcome.

Solid covers in that window are correct rather than a fallback. The same rule applies to number posts and to anything whose cover image lacks a clean licence. Three different reasons, one design outcome, and the renderer treats all three the same way: no image, an ink block, a title, a fixed sub-line. The renderer treats a missing licence and a mourning morning the same way, which is the point of having tokens at all.

The linter enforces the mourning rules rather than trusting a writer to remember them. A mourning post carrying a cover image fails. A mourning post whose tokens are not the greyscale pair raises a warning with the values printed. Neither check is clever. Both catch the mistake a person makes at one in the morning while queueing a post. Both of those checks exist because a writer at one in the morning is the weakest part of the system.

Which leaves one gap, and it is worth naming rather than papering over. The tool tells you today's status when you run it. Nothing runs it for you. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether the render workflow should check the mourning window and fail a non-mourning post inside it]]. That is a design decision the operator should make awake. A habit is a person remembering; a gate is a build that stops.

A reasonable version of that check is easy to describe and left unimplemented on purpose. The workflow calls the mourning tool, and if the window is open while a post marked ready has mourning set to zero, it stops the build and prints both dates. Workable is not finished, and the difference is written down here rather than hidden. The unfilled list is the largest single gap in the repository, and it takes ten minutes with a published calendar to close.
The account changes what it looks like for sixty days a year on the authority of a calendar no machine here is allowed to compute, and that restriction is the most deliberate line in the repository.

post.running_head: what a citation actually points at
post.caption:
The Arabic al-Tabari in this corpus carries 6,438 page markers. The
English volume beside it carries none of them. A page number means a
different thing in each, and a citation that does not say which is
pointing at nothing.

slides.body: six thousand four hundred pages
When a slide says page 407, which book is a reader supposed to open?

Start with the number that is easy to state. The Arabic al-Tabari in this corpus carries 6,438 page markers, each of the form PageV08P271, meaning volume 8, page 271. Those markers came from the edition the file names in its own header. A search returns the volume and the page together, so a citation to that text points at a place two other readers could both find, in the same printing, without help.

Now the harder number. The English volume of al-Tabari on the same shelf carries page numbers of its own, set by its own typesetter, which agree with nothing else in the world. Page 15 of Fishbein is page 15 of that printing. A reader with the Arabic cannot use it, and a reader with a different English printing cannot use it either.

Both are page numbers and only one of them is an address. The difference is whether anybody else prints the same numbers. De Goeje's Leiden pagination became an address because translators printed it in their margins for a century. A devotional ebook conversion has numbers because software had to break the text somewhere. Agreement between printings is the only thing that turns a number into a place, and nobody has ever agreed about an ebook conversion.

This corpus holds all three kinds at once, which is why the manifest records the kind of each volume. Print edition, meaning a typeset book whose numbers a second copy would share. Ebook reflowed, meaning numbers that exist only in this file. Scan, meaning page images with no reliable text. Twenty-six volumes, three categories, and the category decides what a citation is worth.

The extraction figures make the split visible. Of the volumes that opened at all, some came out with a printed number readable on almost every page, and others with fewer than half. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the exact count of volumes in each pagination category, from sources/manifest.yaml]]. That distribution is the real map of what this account can cite with confidence. Which volumes fall into which category is the real map of what this account can cite without hedging, and the manifest is where that map lives.

Where a number could not be read, the tool did not invent one. It looked at the pages on either side, took the offset they agreed on, and marked the result derived rather than read. Where even that failed it wrote nothing and the search prints a question mark. A page marked with a question mark cannot carry a verified claim, by rule.

That rule has an arithmetic behind it worth stating on a number card. Every claim needs one source, one edition and one printed page: three fields, and a row missing any of the three is refused. There is no fourth field for confidence, no partial credit, and no flag anywhere in the tooling that turns the refusal off. A busy evening is when a system with partial credit in it starts producing citations nobody can follow.

Two dates bound this whole problem, and both sit in the fetch tool. 1929 is the cutoff below which an archive.org imprint counts as public domain here. 1879 is the year of the de Goeje volume this pipeline downloaded, which is 50 years the safe side of it. Two dates, one subtraction, and a rule that needs no lawyer to apply.

The download succeeded and the text failed. De Goeje's Arabic came back as Latin noise, and so did Wustenfeld's Yaqut of 1866. Both are registered with usable set to false and a note explaining why. A corpus that records its own failures is a corpus a second person can work in without repeating them. Recording a failure costs one line in a manifest and saves the next person the afternoon it took to find it.

So the honest count for this account is smaller than the shelf suggests. Twenty-six registered volumes, several unusable, several more with pagination that means nothing outside their own file, and one Arabic chronicle with 6,438 real page markers that almost nothing else here can cross-check. [[NEEDS CLAIM: how many of the registered volumes have a filled edition statement]]. Today the answer is one.
A page number is a promise that two people holding different copies will land on the same sentence, and most of the numbers in this corpus cannot keep it.

post.running_head: an argument with three branches and one conclusion
post.cover_title: a boy answers a question about sin
post.caption:
A man on the road asks a boy where sin comes from. The boy gives him a
three-part disjunction, eliminates two branches, and keeps the third. Then
he gives his name: Musa b. Ja'far.

Tuhaf al-'Uqul preserves the argument in the questioner's own voice.

slides.body: a boy answers a question about sin
What does an argument look like when the person making it is a child?

The report comes to us from the man who lost it. He is on his way to see Abu 'Abd Allah Ja'far, he meets a boy, and something the boy says stops him. He asks the boy's name and gets a lineage back: Musa b. Ja'far b. Muhammad b. 'Ali b. al-Husayn b. 'Ali b. Abi Talib. Then he asks the question he had been carrying, about where acts of disobedience come from.

The answer arrives as a disjunction with three branches. The source of any sin, the boy says, is one of three: God, or God and the servant together, or the servant alone. Nothing has been argued yet. The move is to close the space first, so that whatever follows has nowhere else to go, and a listener who accepts the three has already accepted the shape.

Branch one goes first. If God is the source, the boy says, then it is improper for him to punish servants for what they did not commit. That is an argument from the character of the punisher rather than from the mechanics of the act. It rests on something the questioner already holds, which is that the punishment is just.

Branch two goes next, and its reasoning changes register. If God and the servant are partners in the act, then it is improper for the stronger partner to wrong the weaker. Now the vocabulary is contract law: two parties, unequal power, an obligation on the stronger one. The argument has moved from theology to partnership without announcing the move. Partnership language brings its own obligations, and the boy is using them against the second branch rather than against the first.

Branch three is left standing, and the boy takes it. If the servant is the source, then the Lord may pardon out of generosity or may punish for what was committed. Notice that the conclusion does not claim the servant acts alone in the world. It claims only that the servant is where the responsibility sits when a punishment is handed down.

That is a narrow conclusion, placed with care, and the narrowness is what makes the argument survive contact with an opponent. A wider claim about human freedom would have to answer questions about power and knowledge that the three branches never raise. [[NEEDS CLAIM: which theological school this argument is answering, and the source that identifies it]]. He declines to raise them. That restraint is what keeps the conclusion standing when somebody pushes back on it.

The questioner's reaction is the second half of the report. He says the wording was enough for him, and that he turned back without going on to meet the father at all. A man who abandons the errand he set out on is reporting a defeat. Reports of that shape survive because the person who lost the exchange chose to keep telling it.

Which is worth holding onto when reading anything in a collection like this. The chain runs through the man who was answered. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the full chain al-Harrani gives for this report, Tuhaf p. 126]]. If the chain begins with him, the story is a self-report of being outargued, and that is a different kind of evidence from a partisan writing up his own side.

The age of the speaker is doing rhetorical work and should be named as such. A child producing a formal disjunction is a topos, and topoi travel well because they are satisfying to retell. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether any earlier source carries the same three-branch argument, attributed to anybody]]. If the argument predates the attribution, the report tells us about transmission rather than about a boy. Topoi travel because they are satisfying to retell. Test the topos anyway, because a satisfying story is the kind that gets attached to a famous name later.

None of that makes the argument worse as an argument, and this account keeps the two questions apart on purpose. Whether the reasoning holds is a matter anybody can test on the page in front of them. Whether a particular person said it at a particular age is a matter for chains, dates and rijal, and the two questions have different answers. One question is settled by reading. This shelf holds neither the rijal literature nor the dictionaries, so the second question stays open here while the first can be settled by anyone with the page.
The man who wrote this down had ridden out to ask a scholar a question, and he went home because a child had closed it.

post.running_head: the question he declined to take
post.caption:
Abu Ahmad al-Khurasani asks Musa b. Ja'far whether atheism came before
polytheism. The answer is not an answer: you have not been accustomed to
ask such questions, and I do not know that you go in for theological
argument.

Al-Harrani kept the refusal, which is stranger than keeping a reply.

slides.body: you never ask such questions
Why would a collection of teachings preserve a teacher refusing to teach?

Abu Ahmad al-Khurasani puts a clean theological question: did atheism come before polytheism, or the other way round. It is the kind of question that has a structure and a literature behind it, and a man who asks it is signalling that he has read something. The reply does not touch the content at all. You have not been accustomed to ask such questions, Musa b. Ja'far says. Content was never the subject.

Then a second clause, sharper than the first. I do not know that you intrude yourself into theological discussions. That is a statement about the questioner rather than about the question, and it is delivered in front of whoever else was standing there. The subject has been changed from cosmology to the man asking, and the change is the whole event.

Al-Harrani prints this in a collection of maxims and wisdom, where every other entry hands the reader something to carry away. [[NEEDS CLAIM: how many entries in this section end without a teaching, Tuhaf p. 126]]. A compiler assembling useful sayings had no obvious reason to keep a rebuff, which is why keeping it is worth a carousel. Every other entry in the section hands a reader something to carry away, and this one hands them a closed door.

One reading is that the rebuff is the teaching. A man asks a question above his usual level and is told to attend to the level he is at. Read that way, the report is about the danger of speculative argument for somebody without the training to hold it, and it earns its place in a wisdom collection on the same terms as any other entry.

A second reading is political and needs care. Theological disputation in those decades ran alongside real factional lines, and the wrong position argued in the wrong room had consequences for a household already under surveillance. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the sources say about the risks of kalam disputation under Harun al-Rashid]]. On that reading the refusal is prudence rather than pedagogy.

A third reading is simplest and hardest to check: the man asked in bad faith. Somebody arriving with a set question, from a province, to a man whose visitors were watched, might be collecting a position rather than seeking one. [[NEEDS CLAIM: who Abu Ahmad al-Khurasani was, and whether he appears elsewhere in the corpus]]. Nothing on this shelf decides between the three, and a slide that picks one has stopped reporting.

This account cannot choose between those three readings from the material on the shelf, and it will not pretend otherwise. What it can do is set them out, name what each would need to be confirmed, and leave a reader holding three live options instead of one confident sentence. That is a slower carousel and an honest one. The half we have is the refusal; the half we lack is the reply to it.

The report does not end at the refusal. Abu Ahmad confesses something in reply, and the confession is where the passage on this shelf breaks off in the extraction. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what Abu Ahmad al-Khurasani confesses, Tuhaf p. 126 continuing]]. A missing second half is a real limit and naming it is cheaper than working around it. A page break is a property of a typesetter, and an extraction inherits every one of them.

That limit is a property of the pipeline rather than of the book. The text came out of a PDF page by page, and a page break lands where the typesetter put it. A reader with the printed volume turns the page. An extraction inherits every page break the typesetter chose, and a reader has to notice when an argument runs over one.

Which is a small confession of the account's own method. Everything here is read through a page index built by a script from a scan, and the index is honest about which numbers it read and which it derived. It cannot be honest about a sentence that continues past the edge of the page it captured. The only variable in the record is the man being addressed.

Set the refusal beside the letter to Hisham b. al-Hakam and the pair makes a shape. To one correspondent, a long argument about the mind, sent as a letter. To another, a flat instruction to stay out of theological discussion. Same speaker, opposite advice, and the difference between the two is the two men. Two decisions by one man about who gets an argument, and no compiler in the chain remarks on either.

A teaching that varies with the student is either pedagogy or inconsistency, and a collection like this one gives a reader no way to tell which. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether al-Harrani or any later compiler comments on the tension between these two reports]]. A compiler's silence is not agreement, and it is not disagreement either. A refusal from a man that careful is a choice with reasons behind it rather than an absence of one.

The pattern turns up in the biographical material too. Al-Mufid's chapter shows a man who arranges his own burial, refuses a jailer's offer, and says little in public. A person who chose his words with that much care is a person for whom a refusal to answer is a choice with reasons behind it rather than an absence of one. Reconstruction is allowed on a slide as long as the slide says that is what it is.

Reading it that way is a reconstruction and this account marks it as one. What survives on the page is short and can be stated without any reconstruction at all: a man asked a question about atheism and polytheism, and the man he asked told him he was out of his depth, and somebody thought the exchange worth writing down.

Worth writing down is the phrase to end on. Everything in this corpus passed that test at least once, in somebody's hands, for reasons that are invisible now. A report that teaches nothing survived because a compiler judged it useful, and asking what he thought it was useful for is a better question than asking whether it happened. What a compiler thought a report was for is a better question than whether it happened.
He answered a question about the mind at length and refused a question about the origin of unbelief in one sentence, and both refusals are sitting in the same book.

slides.body: the visitor who got up early
What does a poem about a journey tell you that a chronicle does not?

The poem gives instructions to a courier. It addresses a visitor who got up early, ran, and walked like lightning when it flashes, and it asks him to recite the poet's greetings to his master al-Rida, who is at Tus. The grammar is practical throughout: an addressee, an errand, a destination, and a message to deliver on arrival. Nobody writes a courier's poem for a road nobody travels.

Practical instructions imply a practice. Nobody writes a courier's poem for a journey nobody makes, and nobody names a destination that the audience cannot place. The poem assumes a road to Tus, travellers on it, and a shared understanding of what a person does at the other end. All of that sits under the verse without being argued for. The audience is expected to know where Tus is and what a person does on arrival.

Tus is in Khurasan, hundreds of miles east of the Iraqi cities where most of this account's material was written. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the road distance from Baghdad to Tus, and the source]]. That gap is the reason the poem exists: a poet who could go himself would not need to send greetings with somebody else. A poet who could ride there himself would not be handing his greetings to a stranger.

Distance also explains the compiler standing behind the page. Ibn Babawayh names himself as Abu Ja'far Muhammad b. 'Ali b. Husayn b. Musa b. Babwaih al-Qumi, a resident of Ray. Qum is his family's town, Ray is where he lives, and the grave he is writing about is further east again. A book assembled across three places for readers in all of them.

Mourning posts in this account run solid covers on a night ground, and this is one of them. The reason is a rule about the calendar rather than about the subject. [[NEEDS CLAIM: whether the wafat of al-Rida falls inside Muharram and Safar or on the wafat list]]. The design does not decide when to mourn. A published calendar does, and it is not filled in yet.

What the poem preserves better than any chronicle is the traffic. A chronicle records a death, a place, sometimes a cause. It has no field for the fact that people kept arriving afterwards, year after year, in numbers large enough that a poet could assume one of them would carry a message for him. A shrine with a road attached is an economy before anybody calls it an institution.

Traffic is a political fact as well as a devotional one. Travellers on a long road need lodging, guides, water and safe passage, and somebody profits from providing all four. [[NEEDS CLAIM: what the sources say about the road to Tus and the facilities on it in the third century AH]]. A shrine with a road is an economy before anyone calls it an institution.

The second thing the poem carries is a title. It calls him al-Rida, and the book's first chapter opens by asking why that name attached to him. Poems circulate faster than treatises, so a title in verse is evidence that the name was in ordinary use, whatever the argument about its origin concluded. Verse moves faster than a treatise, and it carries a title into places an argument never reaches.

The poem's own attribution needs establishing before any of that stands. [[NEEDS CLAIM: the poet's name and dates, from this edition]]. A verse by a contemporary is a witness. A verse by somebody writing two centuries later is evidence about the later period, which is a different carousel with a different claim on the same page. A witness and a piece of later evidence are two different things wearing the same words.

Neither version is useless, and the difference decides the wording of every slide above. This is why the manifest keeps a field for the edition and refuses verification without it. A poem with no date is a sentence floating free, and a sentence floating free can be made to support almost any argument somebody wants from it. A sentence with no date attached can be made to support almost anything somebody wants from it.

For a mourning post the restraint matters twice over. The subject is a death and a grave, the audience is a community that marks both, and the temptation to write past the evidence is strongest where the feeling runs highest. The design goes quiet on those days. The prose should do the same thing. The design goes quiet on those days, and the prose has to match it or the quiet means nothing.
A poet who could not make the journey handed his greetings to somebody who could, and that arrangement is the whole of what this page proves.
